items.title: General Atomics Offers First Glimspe of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft. The post General Atomics Offers First Glimspe of Wildfire Drone, Eyed as MQ-9 Successor appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

General Atomics has unveiled the first renderings of its Wildfire drone, which it plans to pitch for the Air Force’s hunt for a new, low-cost Massed Modular Aircraft .

Wildfire was unveiled in a sizzle reel-type video General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. posted on social media Sept. 9. The video touts more than three decades of the company’s unmanned aerial vehicle development, starting with the Gnat and Predator drones flown in the 1990s up to and including its latest FQ-42A Dark Merlin, before revealing the first three images of Wildfire in short succession.

The images provide hints of the drone’s expected capabilities. One image shows Wildfire carrying four Joint Strike Missiles, which are stealthy cruise missiles, and another shows it with two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, or LRASMs.

“The whole point of a flying weapons truck is to come heavy,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in response to Air & Space Forces Magazine questions. “Wildfire will be able to carry a minimum of two LRASMs, four JSMs, or some similar configuration of heavy stand-off weapons, across meaningful combat distances.”

Brinkley said the MQ-9A is not be able to carry those payloads, and that they’re twice as much as the Pentagon originally envisioned for MMA. Brinkley said it’s too soon to sat how many Hellfire missiles—which the MQ-9A frequently employs—the Wildfire drone will be able to carry.

A third image shows a swarm of nearly a dozen Wildfire drones bearing down on a group of enemy ships and firing a barrage of missiles at them.

The Air Force envisions Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA , as a low-cost drone to take on missions now done by General Atomics’ MQ-9A, and wants MMA to be semi-autonomous and able to be sent in groups to overwhelm enemy defenses.

Top Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that they want the MMA’s air vehicle—not counting sensors or other capabilities—to cost no more than $10 million apiece. This would allow MMA to be “attritable,” meaning they would be inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.

The Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit, when unveiling the MMA concept in July, said losing $30 million drones in battle against an enemy would be unsustainable in a large-scale conflict, and a less expensive option is needed.

The conflict with Iran has cost the Air Force about 45 of its MQ-9 drones. In the Sept. 3 briefing, Air Force officials said the MQ-9 losses were concerning enough to push the service to accelerate its MMA effort. The Air Force and DIU want to have a prototype MMA a year after is contract is awarded and to start fielding it at scale within three years, or as early as 2029.

General Atomics created Wildfire as a clean-sheet design, and said it will be able to achieve all the Air Force’s MMA requirements at a high quality and an affordable price.

Brinkley said Wildfire will be able to exceed the Air Force and DIU’s 8,000 nautical mile ferry range requirement for MMA.

It will be modular, which will allow the Air Force to rapidly add or swap out different capabilities. When asked about Wildfire’s sensing capabilities, Brinkley said it will have “certain features available right out of the box,” but it will be up to the Air Force to decide what modular capabilities it wants to add.

“Modularity is key,” Brinkley said. “We’re showing that now with our Gambit series of uncrewed jets, which includes the XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station and FQ-42A Collaborative Combat Aircraft. One design, seamlessly pivoting to various missions. Wildfire will be able to do much the same from an [intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]/strike lane.”

Brinkley said General Atomics will use its experience on autonomy, artificial intelligence, and machine learning from its work on programs like CCA and the MQ-20 Avenger, “to network dozens of Wildfires together on Day One.”

Brinkley said General Atomics has more than 5 million square feet of manufacturing space it could leverage to build Wildfire, and that the company has produced up to 100 aircraft per year, including MQ-9s.

“We have said from the beginning that we can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the [Air Force and DIU’s original] fiscal 2031 timeline,” Brinkley said. “We can deliver more than twice as many aircraft as originally asked for in the same amount of time. We’re not worried about scaling at all.”

items.title: Israeli-based defense company rebrands American subsidiary to Twenty-Six Defense
items.author: Leigh Giangreco
items.summary: The U.S. arm of Israeli-based Elbit Systems has rebranded to Twenty-Six Defense, a new name that emphasizes the subsidiary’s American-made brand.
items.body:
MilTech

Israeli-based defense company rebrands American subsidiary to Twenty-Six Defense

A U.S. soldier showcases Elbit America's Enhanced Night Vision Goggle-Binocular (ENVG-B) system. (Elbit America)

The U.S. arm of Israeli-based Elbit Systems has rebranded to Twenty-Six Defense, a new name that emphasizes the subsidiary’s American-made brand.

“Launching Twenty-Six Defense underscores our growth in the American market and reinforces our commitment to supporting U.S. warfighters, wherever the mission takes place,” Luke Savoie, president and CEO of Twenty-Six Defense, said in a company statement on Tuesday.

The number 26 refers to the atomic number for iron and is meant to symbolize “resilience and durability,” Savoie said.

The branding change also comes as American support has become divided in the wake of Hamas’ attack on Israel in October 2023 and the ensuing war in Gaza, which the United Nations classified as a genocide in 2025 .

Headquartered in Fort Worth, Texas, Twenty-Six Defense employs 3,300 people across the United States, according to the company. After General Dynamics sold its tactical aircraft division to Lockheed Martin in 1993, Elbit Systems of America purchased the former General Dynamics manufacturing facility in Fort Worth.

From its Texas headquarters, the company began working on F-16 avionics for the U.S. Air Force. Over the last three decades, the U.S. subsidiary acquired six defense companies, expanding its footprint to include aircraft helmet-mounted display technologies, night vision systems, precision-guided seekers and laser targeting systems.

In 2019, Elbit’s U.S. arm bought Harris Corp’s night vision business as part of an antitrust remedy when Harris and L3 Technologies merged.

Beyond its defense capabilities, Twenty-Six Defense has grown its domestic business in the U.S. as well. In July, the company announced that it scored multiple contracts valued at more than $370 million from the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency. That work is scheduled through May 2029. The U.S. subsidiary has long provided surveillance systems for CBP along the U.S.-Mexico border .

items.title: SOMETIMES THE CALL TO SERVE COMES LATER THAN YOU THINK
items.author: Daniel Rachal
items.summary: Dr. Jeff Crapper, an educator and volunteer fire fighter from Dayton, Oregon, joins the US Navy in the Chaplain Corps at 48-years-old.
items.body:
by Dan Rachal

NTAG Portland Public Affairs

If Dr\. Jeff Crapper would have raised his right hand right after graduating high school and enlisted in the United States Navy, he could have retired this year\. In almost Benjamin Button fashion, he is beginning his Navy career in reverse\. On Aug\. 11, 2026, at 48\-years\-old, he was sworn into the United States Navy as an officer in the Chaplain Corps\. Crapper noted that, while he was starting a Navy career later in life, it is because he has a desire to be of service to people\.

“I am looking to challenge myself at the highest level while making a tangible difference in the lives of Sailors and Marines,” he said. “I want to grow in my own faith and leadership by mentoring others through their hardest moments.”

Crapper said it took over a year and a half, and tested the limits of his resilience and dedication, before being selected as an officer in the Chaplain Corps. He was not chosen on his initial application and had to obtain a second master’s degree and an age waiver, before being selected on his second attempt.

After high school, Crapper originally wanted to compete at Linfield University in McMinnville, Oregon, his father’s Alma Mater, in track and field. As an athlete at West Albany High School in Albany, Oregon. Crapper was one of the top discus throwers in the nation. Unfortunately, a serious knee injury altered those plans. He still attended Linfield, triple majoring in sports medicine, health education and exercise science.

Shortly after graduating in 2001, he began working with the Sherwood School District in Sherwood, Oregon. In 2020, because of a shortage of first responders during COVID, he began as a volunteer firefighter in Dayton, Oregon. In 2021, he started working as a member of the Beaverton School District crisis response team.

On July 27, 2026, Chief Navy Counselor Tiffany Colburn, his recruiter at Navy Talent Acquisition Group Portland, called Crapper to let him know the good news – his application was selected. When she reached him, he wasn’t on summer vacation with family or getting ready for the school year, he was in northern Oregon fighting the Hagen fire, which was burning 26,000 acres at the time.

“I gave him a call and woke him up in the middle of his sleep,” Colburn said. “Honestly, I wouldn’t expect anything else from him. He’s always doing everything he can, so it’s not surprising. He’s fighting fires until two or three days before he ships out.”

So, while being amid a literal fire, Crapper learned he would go into another profession at a time when, according to a 2022 Stanford Center on Longevity Report, Americans are beginning to plan for retirement. To him, this is not about starting anew but rather taking his decades of experience, resilience and faith to make a meaningful difference with those who serve.

“I’ve served on the front lines as both a firefighter and a member of a school district crisis response team and spent my career running toward situations where most people flee, which has given me a practical, grounded approach to spiritual leadership and to supporting others through their darkest hours,” Crapper said. “I aspire to craft a story that demonstrates that it’s never too late to pursue a new path of service and impact.”

Navy Talent Acquisition Group Portland is headquartered in Portland, Oregon, and

operates two Navy Officer Recruiting stations and 17 Navy Recruiting stations locatedthroughout northern California, western Idaho, Oregon, northern Nevada and southernWashington, covering more than 210,000 square miles. NTAG Portland is staffed withmore than 130 Sailors and civilians whose mission is the recruitment of high-qualitymen and women to fill the officer and enlisted ranks in the U.S. Navy. Follow NTAGPortland on Facebook and Instagram @ntagportland.

items.title: Free fall school trains students in high-altitude infiltration
items.author: K. Kassens
items.summary: Story by K. Kassens, U.S. Army John F. items.body: YUMA PROVING GROUND, Ariz. - Joint-forces students attending the Military Free Fall School are reaching new heights as they qualify in advanced high-altitude insertion techniques at one of the Army’s toughest advanced courses. The Military Free Fall School (MFFS), located at the U.S. Army’s Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, is an elite joint-forces institution operated by the U.S. Army John F.Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School. The school trains special operations forces in critical infiltration skills, including high-altitude low-opening (HALO) and high-altitude high-opening (HAHO) parachuting. “We train Department of War and other agencies’ personnel to conduct airborne infiltrations,” said Sgt. Maj. Zachary Achziger, MFFS’ senior enlisted leader under the 2nd Special Warfare Training Group (Airborne). The military free-fall program traces its roots to March 1957 when the 77th Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, conducted the first basic body-stabilization free-fall course.This evolved into the formal HALO project in 1958. The official Military Free Fall School graduated its first class at Fort Bragg on Aug. 13, 1971, before moving operations to Yuma Proving Ground. Students from across the military services master one of the most demanding skills in the military. The students learn advanced parachuting techniques and tactical infiltration methods to jump into sensitive areas undetected from altitudes up to 25,000 feet. “This course gives an operator the skill set of airborne infiltration that allows geographic combatant commanders more flexibility on how to employ special operations forces,” Achziger said. “It gives those geographic combatant commanders options to extend their range to infiltrate someone into far away areas.” To qualify for attendance, students must be a graduate of basic U.S. Army Airborne School, hold a designated free fall-coded position, such as special operations, select riggers, or approved allied Department of War personnel and meet strict Class 3 flight physical and medical standards for high-altitude oxygen use. Before climbing aboard an aircraft, students begin their training by packing their main parachute, while qualified riggers pack the reserve parachutes. Next, students learn the fundamentals of body position and stability during training in a controlled environment as they learn to fly their bodies in the Master Sgt. George Bannar Vertical Wind Tunnel. The presence of the vertical wind tunnel, which opened at Yuma Proving Ground in early 2014, has become a crucial tool for students who attend the course. The 16.5-foot tunnel allows students to practice maintaining a stable body position and learn how to make small adjustments with their arms and legs and, ultimately, gaining the muscle memory needed once they jump from an aircraft. The progression is deliberate. Students learn how to control their bodies, then practice those skills in a simulated environment before taking them into the air. “The wind tunnel allows us to give students increased time with training their free fall skills before their first jump and as a tool for remedial training,” Achziger said. “It has also increased our overall capabilities to train without having to use an aircraft.” For Sgt. Maj. Matthew Krueger, an instructor at the school, he said that the wind tunnel is a great training tool. “With it, the students are able to recover from tumbling much faster and gets them ready for the harder parts of the course when we introduce equipment,”he said. After mastering the basics of free fall in the wind tunnel, the students make their first jumps with a highly skilled instructor. During the four-week course, instructors evaluate students aircraft exit to landing on the drop zone. Students make most of their jumps from the C-27J Spartan, a smaller cargo plane that uses the same engine as its larger cousin, the C-130 Hercules. Jumps are conducted from altitudes ranging from 9,500 to 25,000 feet, depending on the training requirement. To qualify for the course, a prospective student must have completed at least five static line jumps, though most students have completed more. The course exposes students to a variety of equipment and conditions. They practice jumping with and without weapons and combat equipment, as well as with night vision goggles and supplemental oxygen. They conduct jumps during both daylight and nighttime conditions, requiring them to apply their skills while adapting to various wind conditions and changing environments. “The students add one piece at a time and get evaluated throughout the course before moving to the next graded exercise,” Achziger said. “They are graded on everything - slick jumps, combat equipment, night jumps, everything.” Achziger said that following the jumps they move into the grouping phase. “Then they learn and train on weapons integration,” he said. “Also, during the grouping phase, students train for “stand-offs,” which include high-altitude high opening jumps during both day and night conditions.” After jumping, students execute free-fall techniques before deploying their parachutes and descending toward Phillips Drop Zone at Yuma Proving Ground. Instructors have the ability to talk to students on two-way radios to assist them on how and where to land. By the completion of the Basic Military Free Fall Course, students will have developed the foundation needed to conduct military free-fall operations from high altitude, while using the specialized gear required for operational missions. The school also trains and qualifies select students for the Military Free Fall Jumpmaster Course, the Advanced Tactical Infiltration Course and the Military Free Fall Instructor Course. Those with higher levels of free-fall experience can return to Yuma Proving Ground and attend the Advanced Tactical Infiltration Course, which focuses on HAHO, navigation, complex mission planning, and execution under canopy. The Military Free Fall Instructor Course selects elite, seasoned operators with hundreds of jumps to earn a rare Department of War instructor rating, so that they can forge the next generation of free-fall service members. “For Green Berets, Air Force special operations, Marine special ops and Navy SEALs, it’s a unique method to get to work,”Krueger said. “It’s a great infiltration technique, especially for an ODA [Operational Detachment Alpha] where they can exit an aircraft, fly together in a group in a standoff, and land on target ready to carry out a mission.”

items.title: USS Beloit (LCS 29) Namesake Visit
items.author: LTJG Riley Gavigan
items.summary: Sailors assigned to the Freedom-Variant Littoral Combat Ship USS Beloit (LCS 29) visited their ship’s namesake city September 4-6, 2026.
items.body:
BELOIT, WI (September 6, 2026) - U.S. Navy Sailors from the Freedom class littoral combat ship USS Beloit (LCS 29) traveled to Beloit, Wisconsin, over Labor Day weekend to honor the ship’s namesake city and strengthen ties with the community through a series of engagements with local residents, students, veterans, and city leaders.

Beloit is one of the smallest cities in America to have a U.S. Navy warship named in its honor, a recognition of the city’s outsized contribution to the nation’s defense industry over generations. Commissioned November 23, 2024, in Milwaukee, USS Beloit is the first commissioned Navy ship to bear the city’s name, and Wisconsin leaders have pointed to the state’s long shipbuilding legacy as central to that honor. The ship’s motto, “Forward for Freedom,” reflects both its Freedom class heritage and its ties to the Wisconsin community that shares its name.

“We are so fortunate to have a close-knit community in Beloit, Wisconsin who continues to support not only our ship, but also other US Navy platforms that have engines manufactured in Beloit. The Beloit residents welcomed us with open arms.” said Cmdr. Jason DeJesus Commanding Officer, USS Beloit (LCS 29). “We are so lucky to have our USS Beloit Legacy Foundation that scheduled multiple events across the city ensuring there was an opportunity for everyone to interact with the crew.”

Seven Sailors from USS Beloit arrived in the city on Friday, September 4, kicking off a weekend of engagement events. On Saturday, September 5, the crew began the day with a meet-and-greet with the public at the Beloit Farmer’s Market, hosted alongside the Downtown Beloit Association. In the afternoon, Sailors played pickleball with community members at Wooten Park before heading to The Lincoln Academy for a tour and meeting with the school’s Navy Junior ROTC Cadets. The evening capped off with “USS Beloit Night” at a Beloit Sky Carp baseball game, where Sailors sat alongside members of the local VFW and NJROTC unit and met with fans.

On Sunday, September 6, the crew visited Beloit Senior Living to spend time with WWII veteran George Olson, joined by members of the veteran support organization VetsRoll. Later that morning, Sailors visited Turtle Island playground to spend time with local children before a scheduled afternoon visit with leadership and members of the local VFW chapter.

USS Beloit is designed as a fast, agile, mission-focused platform built for operation in near-shore environments while remaining capable of open-ocean missions. The ship is capable of supporting forward presence, maritime security, sea control, and deterrence operations. USS Beloit is homeported at Naval Station Mayport, Florida.

items.title: Lt. Col. Earl Promoted, Continues Supporting Madigan Staff, Patients and Readiness
items.author: Joseph Jones
items.summary: MADIGAN ARMY MEDICAL CENTER, Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash. — Madigan Army Medical Center recently celebrated the promotion of one of its most recognizable team members when Earl, a black Labrador retriever who supports staff and patients throughout the medical center, advanced from major to lieutenant colonel. Madigan Director Col. Jimmy Watts presided over the ceremony, recognizing Earl’s dedicated service and continued impact across the Madigan community.
items.body:
MADIGAN ARMY MEDICAL CENTER, Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Wash. — Madigan Army Medical Center recently celebrated the promotion of one of its most recognizable team members when Earl, a black Labrador retriever who supports staff and patients throughout the medical center, advanced from major to lieutenant colonel.

Madigan Director Col. Jimmy Watts presided over the ceremony, recognizing Earl’s dedicated service and continued impact across the Madigan community.

"As our facility dog, Earl provides a very special kind of care that medicine alone cannot replicate," said Watts. "Whether sitting with a patient before a procedure or giving our healthcare staff a moment of relief during a grueling shift, Earl brings comfort, boosts morale, and strengthens the heart of our facility. Promoting him to lieutenant colonel is our way of honoring his faithful service to the entire Madigan family."

Earl arrived at Madigan in May 2022 and received his first honorary rank of captain that July. He was later promoted to major on May 31, 2024. Since arriving at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Earl has become a beloved fixture throughout the hospital corridors, actively bolstering staff wellness and comforting patients and their families.

Earl works closely alongside his handler, Ms. Tracy Baker, Madigan’s Healthcare Resolution Specialist. Together, they provide health care professionals with dedicated peer support and wellness initiatives while conducting routine rounds across clinical and administrative workspaces.

"Earl brings an immediate sense of calm and relief wherever he goes," said Baker. "Our healthcare teams face immense pressure daily, and having Earl step into a ward allows staff a crucial moment to pause, breathe, and reset before returning to their vital work."

Connecting wellness to mission readiness

For a military medical treatment facility, staff wellness is inextricably linked to mission readiness. Healthcare professionals routinely operate in high-tempo, demanding clinical environments, caring for service members and families during critical and vulnerable moments. Ensuring staff have structured opportunities to decompress, process stress, and maintain emotional resilience directly supports overall operational effectiveness.

"Readiness starts with taking care of our caregivers," Baker noted. "Earl’s role isn’t just about providing comfort; it’s an active intervention that strengthens resilience across our medical teams so they can continue delivering the highest standard of care."

Impact across wards and waiting areas

Beyond supporting hospital staff, Earl’s daily rounds bring comfort and positive distraction to patients facing challenging medical circumstances. His calm temperament helps alleviate anxiety during appointments, procedures, and extended inpatient stays.

"When patients see Earl, the entire atmosphere changes," Baker added. "He helps break down the stress and apprehension often associated with medical visits, fostering a much more healing and supportive environment."

Although Earl’s military rank is honorary, the vital role he performs reflects Madigan’s broader commitment to total workforce wellness and patient-centered care. Now proudly serving as Lt. Col. Earl, he will continue his regular rounds across the facility, sustaining the resilience and readiness of the Madigan health care team.

items.title: Fort Buchanan Newcomers Fair connects people, resources to strengthen readiness
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Soldiers, future Soldiers, civilian employees and other members of the military community participated in Fort Buchanan’s Newcomers Fair Sept. 9 at the installation Community Club, allowing participants to establish points of contact and learn how to access resources across the Army’s home in the Caribbean.
items.body: FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — Soldiers, future Soldiers, civilian employees and other members of the military community participated in Fort Buchanan’s Newcomers Fair Sept. 9 at the installation Community Club, allowing participants to establish points of contact and learn how to access resources across the Army’s home in the Caribbean. Ulises Marrero, Fort Buchanan acting garrison manager, said those connections are an important part of becoming a member of the installation community. “Fort Buchanan is a family, and I don’t get tired of saying that,” Marrero said. “Whatever you need, you need to know who provides that service, and this is the opportunity for you.” The Newcomers Fair emphasized direct interaction between participants and the people who provide services across the installation. For Tara Ulrich, an Antilles Middle School teacher from Grand Forks, North Dakota, who recently moved to Puerto Rico, the event helped her become familiar with her new workplace and community. “When you first start, everything’s a whirlwind, so having a little time here and getting to learn about all the services available is really beneficial,” Ulrich said. The fair also reached future Soldiers before they depart Puerto Rico for initial military training. Alishka Rivera, a future Soldier from San Juan who is scheduled to depart for training in January, attended the event to familiarize herself with the Army community and its resources. “I think this is a great opportunity to learn about all the services Fort Buchanan has to offer and to better understand the resources available to us,” Rivera said. Sandra Valerio González, a future Soldier from Camuy who is scheduled to depart for initial military training in October, also used the fair to learn about services available as she begins her Army career. “As someone who recently joined, I didn’t know what services, facilities or options were available to us,” Valerio González said. “This is a great opportunity because now we can learn about those resources.” Their participation highlighted how Fort Buchanan can connect future Soldiers with the Army support network even before they leave for training. Those connections contribute to readiness. When Soldiers know where to obtain assistance, families understand the resources available to them and civilian employees can navigate installation services, the workforce can remain focused on accomplishing the mission. Army Community Service provides programs and resources that support service members, families, retirees and Department of War civilians. Its programs include relocation and employment readiness, financial readiness, family advocacy, mobilization and deployment support, and the Exceptional Family Member Program. As the Army’s home in the Caribbean, Fort Buchanan provides the infrastructure, services and workforce support that enable military forces to train, mobilize and deploy when required. The Newcomers Fair demonstrated that enabling the warfighter starts with ensuring the people behind the mission know their community and can access the resources they need to remain ready. For more information about newcomer resources, contact the Army Community Service Relocation Readiness Program at 787-707-3682 or 787-707-3697. Community members can also download the My Army Post app and select Fort Buchanan for official installation information, services, community resources and real-time updates.

items.title: Fort Sill to host 9/11 Remembrance Run Friday
items.author: Edward Muniz
items.summary: Fort Sill will host its annual 9/11 Remembrance Run/Walk on Friday, Sept. 11, at McNair Hall, inviting the community to gather in remembrance of the lives lost on Sept. 11, 2001.
items.body:
Fires Center of Excellenc and Fort Sill Public Affairs usarmy.sill.fcoe.mbx.pao@army.mil Sept. 9, 2026

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Fort Sill to host 9/11 Remembrance Run Friday

FORT SILL, Okla. — Fort Sill will host its annual 9/11 Remembrance Run/Walk on Friday, Sept. 11, at McNair Hall, inviting the community to gather in remembrance of the lives lost on Sept. 11, 2001.

This year’s observance marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11. Participants may choose from a 4-mile run, 4-mile ruck, or 1-mile fun run/walk. The event will kick off with a reenlistment ceremony at 7:35 a.m., followed by the opening ceremony, salute cannons, remarks from the Fires Center of Excellence Commanding General Brig. Gen. Patrick Costello and then the run will begin promptly at 8:05 a.m.

“On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Fort Sill is honored to bring Soldiers, Families and the surrounding community together to remember those we lost and to reflect on the service and sacrifice that followed,” Col. Jay Morgan said, Fort Sill garrison commander.

Although registration is closed, all are invited to attend and participate. The event is open to the public and free participation is available for all. Organizers encourage anyone who has already registered for the run to pick up registration packets before Friday at the Patriot Club during normal operating hours.

"This run isn't just about fitness—it’s about Family,” Sarah Gersper said, Director of Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation at Fort Sill. “Twenty-five years later, we still run side by side so our Soldiers, Families and neighbors have a shared space to pause, remember and honor the extraordinary sacrifices made that day and every day since."

Participants and visitors should plan and arrive early. Fort Sill expects increased traffic Friday morning due to the remembrance event and unit participation.

Gate Access:

52nd Street Gate – open from 5 a.m. to 9 a.m.

Bentley Gate and Apache Gate – open at 5 a.m.

Scott Gate – open 24 hours.

**** Use of Key Gate East is discouraged unless attending Basic Combat Training graduation.

Visitors without a DoD ID card should obtain a visitor pass from the Fort Sill’s Visitor Welcome Center in advance and be prepared for 100% ID checks at installation entry points.

Parking options include the PX, Commissary, Honeycutt Fitness Center, Patriot Club Field Artillery Museum, Air Defense Artillery Training Support Facility and Twin Oaks Bowling Alley. Attendees should be prepared to walk to McNair Hall.

To facilitate the run and associated 9/11 remembrance activities, Fort Sill residents and visitors should expect road closures and delays from 7 a.m. to 11 a.m. north of Randolph Road and south of Fort Sill Golf Course, particularly in the neighborhoods of White Wolf, Academic Heights and Old Post Quadrangle.

Fort Sill also advises attendees that animals are not permitted at this event and should be left at home.

Prohibited items include:

Backpacks and coolers

Weapons of any kind, including small pocketknives and Leatherman tools

Cannabis and recreational drugs

Laser pointers, fireworks, glass containers and Frisbees

For families at Freedom Elementary School, some bus routes will run 10 minutes earlier that morning. Parents with attendance questions should reference the Freedom Elementary Facebook page or contact the school directly.

Fort Sill appreciates the community’s patience and cooperation as it honors and remembers those lost on Sept. 11.

For more information, call (580) 442-5300 or visit the Fort Sill MWR event page.

— Fires —

items.title: White House sentries recognized for support to national security missions
items.author: CPT Lauri Schleicher
items.summary: WASHINGTON — Five White House sentries assigned to Guard Company, Marine Barracks Washington, received Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medals for their diligent and faithful service, providing more than 1,600 hours of White House security in support of the President of the United States throughout Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Absolute Resolve.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — Five White House sentries assigned to Guard Company, Marine Barracks Washington, received Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medals for their diligent and faithful service, providing more than 1,600 hours of White House security in support of the President of the United States throughout Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Absolute Resolve.

Cpl. Nathaniel Swartwood, Cpl. James McGhee, Cpl. Jaryn CarrilloTalmadge, Cpl. Jeremiah Chancey and Cpl. Alexander Wilson serve with 3rd Platoon, Guard Company. From June 2025 to March 2026, the Marines remained vigilant, ready to respond to any situation at a moment’s notice, including nights, weekends and holidays.

“You understand the significance of the mission every time you stand post at the White House,” said Swartwood, noncommissioned officer in charge of the White House sentries. “A lot of the work happens when no one sees it. You trust the Marines around you, stay ready and do what the mission requires.”

Col. Jason C. Copeland, commanding officer of Marine Barracks Washington, presented the awards in recognition of the Marines’ professionalism, discipline and resilience. Their ability to adapt to changing requirements while maintaining continuous coverage contributed to the successful execution of both operations.

The awards reflect the responsibility entrusted to Guard Company Marines to remain ready when and where they are needed, often with little notice and outside the public eye. Whether safeguarding the “Oldest Post of the Corps” or standing watch in direct support of the President, Barracks Marines demonstrate the discipline and readiness required of Marines in every mission.

items.title: Fort Knox Snaps Army Bowl Drought
items.author: Jedhel Somera
items.summary: In a rivalry shaped by five decades of military heritage, Fort Knox outlasted Fort Campbell 29-23 on Friday night in the 50th Army Bowl.
items.body:
In a rivalry shaped by five decades of military heritage, Fort Knox High School outlasted Fort Campbell High School 29-23 on Friday night in the 50th Army Bowl.

"It is a big rivalry, and these schools mean a lot to their installations," Fort Campbell principal Jaime Romero said. "Just getting them together means a lot to the Army community."

That long-standing connection gives the annual matchup an atmosphere unlike any other in high school football. "This has been going on since the '70s," Fort Campbell head coach Henry Mitchell added. "Both schools have been playing each other for a long time. It is unique, and we take the matchup seriously each time."

Coming into the milestone game, Fort Knox head coach Nick Covin wanted his offense to "score in bunches," hoping for a "good, hard fight" between the two programs. The Eagles delivered early, capitalizing on defensive breakdown and a late takeaway to leap out to a 20-0 lead in the opening quarter.

To spark a turnaround, Mitchell urged his squad to focus on the basics, telling his players to "block and tackle, clean up penalties, be disciplined, play fast and play violent." Romero echoed those thoughts from the sideline, noting that success comes down to simple execution: "Fundamentals. We need to tackle, move the chain, move the ball, and hold on to the ball."

Fort Campbell responded with a fierce second-quarter rally, cutting the deficit to 20-14 behind a quarterback keeper and a fumble recovery in the end zone.

Adversity struck the Eagles midway through the quarter when their starting signal-caller went down with an injury, forcing Fort Knox to adjust its game plan on the fly. The Falcons seized the momentum, stringing together a late drive that capped off with a field goal just before halftime to pull within 20-17.

Defenses dominated the second half in a punishing, back-and-forth battle. Fort Campbell briefly tied the game 23-23 in the fourth quarter after scooping up an Eagles fumble and taking it to the house. However, Fort Knox answered immediately, breaking loose for a long touchdown run to regain the lead. The Falcons mounted one final drive into Eagles territory, but a late turnover on downs sealed the victory for Fort Knox.

The victory handed the Eagles the coveted Army Bowl trophy for the first time in several years, snapping a four-game losing streak to their rival. While Fort Campbell holds a 32-18 lead in the all-time series dating back to 1974.

items.title: Don’t let illness sidetrack the mission: Prepare now for cold and flu season
items.author: Maria Christina Yager
items.summary: FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kansas — While many people are winding down from summer and easing into pumpkin spice season, the health care team at Munson Army Health Center is already preparing the Fort Leavenworth community for cold and flu season.
items.body:
FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kansas — While many people are winding down from summer and easing into pumpkin spice season, the health care team at Munson Army Health Center is already preparing the Fort Leavenworth community for cold and flu season.

Munson’s Public Health team will host an information table at the Fort Leavenworth Commissary from 10:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. Friday, Sept. 18, to share practical steps and resources that can help community members protect their health, care for their families and remain ready for the months ahead.

For students attending the Command and General Staff College, an illness lasting several days can disrupt a demanding schedule of time-sensitive instruction. That impact can be felt whether the student becomes sick or must step away from class to care for an ill child or another family member.

“Cold and flu season can affect an entire household,” said Michelle Grant, Munson Public Health nurse. “Preparing before respiratory illnesses begin circulating more widely can help families protect their health, manage illness at home and reduce the risk of sickness disrupting important family, work and school commitments.”

Most people who contract influenza recover within a few days to less than two weeks, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. However, influenza can cause serious complications, particularly among young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with certain chronic health conditions.

The Munson team will focus on three practical ways community members can prepare: receive an annual influenza vaccination, stock appropriate supplies at home and practice healthy daily habits.

“The best time to prepare for an illness is before someone in your household becomes sick,” Grant said. “Getting vaccinated, keeping basic health supplies on hand and knowing how to access care can make an unexpected illness easier to manage.”

CDC recommends annual influenza vaccination for people 6 months and older who do not have a contraindication. For most people, September or October is an ideal time to receive the vaccine. Munson has ordered seasonal influenza vaccines and plans to administer flu shots through a series of outreach events starting in October, pending availability. Visitors can stop by the information table to learn about seasonal influenza vaccination opportunities available on Fort Leavenworth.

The team will also share information about preparing a home medicine cabinet with items such as a working thermometer, tissues, hydration supplies and appropriate over-the-counter medications for symptom relief. Visitors can learn about Munson’s free over-the-counter medication program and speak with the team about using medications safely.

Additional topics will include proper handwashing, cough etiquette, cleaning frequently touched surfaces and staying home when sick. CDC recommends staying home and away from others while experiencing a respiratory illness and returning to normal activities after symptoms have improved overall and an individual has been fever-free without fever-reducing medication for at least 24 hours.

Community members can learn how to contact the appointment line or the TRICARE Nurse Advice Line when they need guidance about an illness or injury and also learn how to activate prescriptions before arriving at the Munson pharmacy to help reduce wait times.

“We want community members to talk with us now, learn what resources are available and make a plan before illness occurs,” Grant said. “A little preparation can help protect your family and keep cold and flu season from sidetracking your schedule.”

The post Combat Weather Airmen Stressed to Their Limits in Ar
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

In the small world of Air Force weather specialists , combat weather specialists are a niche unto themselves, deploying with Army ground units to provide forecasts and, if need be, fight alongside those Soldiers. For Staff Sgt. Francisco Estrada, the hardest part of the job isn’t the possibility of ground combat, though—it’s briefing Army helicopter pilots on short notice how wind, fog, rain, and other conditions will affect a mission.

Being right about hazardous conditions often means an upcoming flight is scrubbed. Being wrong about them, though, could cause helicopter engines to fail or send an aircrew flying into the side of a mountain.

“Anybody can sit behind a desk and put everything together when they have all the time in the world, but when you are on the fly like you are oftentimes out in the field … it’s really hard to gather everything that you need do it well and do it confidently, when somebody’s asking you, ‘Hey, well, can we can we launch? Can we go?’” Estrada told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Airmen in this unique career field were tested Aug. 12-13 when combat weather squadrons from across the Air Force participated in Thunder Challenge 2026, a physically and mentally challenging competition that this year put six three-Airmen teams from around the world through two days of high-pressure skill tests at Fort Drum, N.Y.

Competitors marched 10 miles, carrying weapons and 35-pound rucksacks. The competition also included a night land navigation course and a simulated mountain rescue on foot through the thick forested terrain.

Skill stations tested everything from small-arms knowledge to combat casualty care—combat-related tasks these Airmen could need at any time since they are attached to Army combat units. In between these tactical tasks, the combat weather Airmen, known as staff weather officers, or SWOs, also had to prove their technical job expertise by completing tasks ranging from setting up portable weather sensors to a timed weather knowledge test.

Thunder Challenge “is the only competition that measures the lethal combination” of tactical skills as well the “environmental science” knowledge needed operate within Army combat units and advise aviators and combat leaders on how changing weather conditions could impact future missions, Chief Master Sergeant Ronald Buchanan of the Air Force’s 5th Combat Weather Group, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“It’s unique because you they go straight from grueling, physical challenges such weighted ruck marches or live-fire stress shooting directly to setting up tactical meteorological equipment, and then from that, using that same equipment or their weather knowledge to deliver an Indo-Pacific-focused forecast brief, not only just under the physical but also under that mental fatigue as well,” Buchanan said.

“These competitions help further prove that we can operate and deliver critical environmental intelligence at the absolute forward edge of any battlefield.”

Estrada, whose team from the 7th Combat Weather Squadron in Germany beat out five other teams to win first place this year, was also part of last year’s winning team at Thunder Challenge. He has been a combat weather specialist for the last three of his seven years in the Air Force. While assigned to the Army’s 12th Combat Aviation Brigade at Katterbach Army Airfield, Estrada has seen a lot of Airmen “get scared” when it comes to preparing an air mission brief on a short deadline with limited data.

During Thunder Challenge, teams had to prepare a brief in about 45 minutes with “very little data, and more importantly, with data from a location that we didn’t know,” Estrada said.

“It’s such a compact timeframe to do that confidently … you have to consider so much. Whether it’s where they’re flying to, their route of flight, are they going over an ocean because at that point, we have to consider what the sea temperatures are like,” Estrada said, adding that headwinds, crosswinds and other conditions that can “make or break their decision to fly, especially when it comes to fuel consumption.”

Normally, SWOs will have at least several hours’ notice, if not a day or two, to prepare a brief and “we’ve had time to kind of do everything and kind of get used to the localized weather pattern,” Estrada said.

Satellite imagery helps with dissecting approaching weather fronts that can bring stormy, wet weather. Topography plays a large role in preparing a brief, Estrada said, especially in the mountains, where low ceilings can be dangerous.

Helicopter pilots have low cloud ceiling minimums they can fly in, “but in those mountains, because they hold so much moisture to trap it all in, it’ll be socked in so you’ll have ceilings go from like 3,000 feet to all of a sudden, your ceilings are on the surface,” Estrada said. “You can’t get through it.”

Army aviators spend a lot of time studying available weather forecasting applications but depend on combat weather Airmen for an unbiased analysis of flying conditions, said UH-60 Black Hawk pilot Capt. Tom Pelkey, who was one of the judges on the air brief portion of the competition.

“You will not launch until the Air Force weather officer gives you a brief,” he said, explaining that Army regulations require it to “ensure that the pilots themselves don’t shop for favorable weather” to suit their mission.

Many factors are needed for a good air brief such as “what’s the moonset going to be if we’re launching at night—like how much illumination? What’s the sea state going to be since we’re flying over water?” said Pelkey, who is assigned to 3rd Battalion, 10th Combat Aviation Brigade at Drum.

Air density is also a critical piece of data helicopter pilots need when planning a mission, Pelkey said. Helicopters need dense air to generate lift through the main rotor blades. Air density decreases with altitude and has an adverse impact on aircraft performance.

“The engine’s going to work based on the density altitude or how much moisture is in the air affected by the temperature, so if it’s going to be hot and moist, my engine doesn’t have much air to beat into combustion,” Pelkey said. “And that’s something helicopter pilots, and even pilots in general, have to be aware of … because that limits us on what the aircraft can carry, how many people we can carry, and what maneuvers we can do.”

When critiquing each team’s air brief, Pelkey said pilots stress that they need combat weather Airmen to provide analysis along with weather data.

“The big thing that we want … the SWOs to understand is, ‘you bring me the weather. All right, so what? What does that mean for my mission exactly?’” Pelkey said. “If we had two routes that we’re going to fly, you need to recommend the route that I’m going to fly based on the weather.”

Sending combat weather Airmen to Thunder Challenge gives leaders an opportunity to gauge the effectiveness of the training that SWOs receive throughout the year, said Col. Staci Coleman, commander of the 5th Combat Weather Group, which commands the 18th Combat Weather Squadron headquartered at of Fort Bragg, N.C., and the 3rd Combat Weather Squadron out of Fort Hood, Texas.

The competition “enables leaders to put the Airmen to the test, so we can see where they’re at with the development of their skills,” Coleman said. “Can they apply their weather expertise and operate as warfighters and make good decisions under pressure? So, we use that as an opportunity to put them under stress just to see how they can respond and to show them where the gaps are in their own training and things that they need to improve on.”

Coleman added that “it shows us where we’re strong and where we need to improve and ensures that we’re building combat-ready Airmen who are ready for the fight.”

To 1st Lt. Isabel Weiss, participating in the competition was a great experience for her “very junior team,” since it was “totally different from what most people think of when they think of the Air Force and when they think of weather support.”

“I think a lot of people think of computer people just looking at models, but it was a really intense competition, and we got to go into the Army combat skills that we’ve learned, and also we got to show our other proficiency,” said Weiss, who is part of an 18th CWS detachment that’s attached to the Army’s 3rd Combat Aviation Brigade at Fort Stewart, Ga. “We were into it; I thought it was amazing.”

Her team came in fourth place, which she is “very proud of” since “we were brand new to this type of competition environment,” said Weiss, who was named Fittest SWO from her combined score on the fitness test, 10-mile ruck march, and mountaineering portion of the competition.

Her team trained at Fort Stewart for the night land navigation, but the course at Drum was “very hard, and it was pitch black,” Weiss said. “We only had red light headlamps, and two of our headlamps died.”

“We were in the trenches for sure, but that was great,” she said. “I really do like this tactical stuff. … We had our face paints on, we had our bulletproof vests and helmets, sleeping outside, shooting weapons; it was just a really cool thing that you don’t get to do very often with the Air Force.”

The competition was also great on-the-job training for her junior Airmen teammates, Weiss said.

“I think the first time that they go to an exercise, or when they get ready for deployment, they’re going to be so familiar with the equipment, when it’s used, how it’s used, and then just working in a high-pressure situation—I think it’s a really unique thing that I’ve never heard of an Airman experiencing so early in their career.”

For Estrada, the hardest field skill was the mountain rescue portion of the competition that required teams to locate a dummy casualty and move “him” through steep, wooded terrain on a “Skedco,” which is a special stretcher equipped with straps for securing a casualty that can be lowered down steep inclines by ropes.

“We had to assess him for any injuries or any wounds, and … then we had to move him in Skedco from point A to point B,” Estrada said. “I think it might have been a good 100 meters, long enough to just be exhausting.” Teams then had to lower the casualty down one cliff and up to the top of another steep rise, he said.

Estrada said he will likely compete in next year’s competition as well. “It gives you an opportunity to kind of gauge where you’re at versus like your peers,” he said. “And I think there’s something rewarding about that—seeing all your effort, all the dedication that you put into your skillset to kind of become a better forecaster, a better combat weather team. There’s something so gratifying about that, that it’s hard to kind of walk away from.”
