items.title: Air University puts chiefs to work on problems without easy answers
items.author: Billy Blankenship
items.summary: The Chief Leadership Academy at Air University, Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama, develops senior enlisted leaders through professional military education focused on strategic thinking, joint operations and leadership beyond their individual career fields. The academy paused its Chief Leadership Course for nine months to rebuild and modernize its curriculum, incorporating input from senior leaders, subject matter experts and graduates before relaunching in June 2025. The redesigned course challen
items.body: MAXWELL AIR FORCE BASE, Ala.— Five minutes before a group of chiefs is supposed to brief, the problem changes. They've been working toward a solution. Now an Airman needs attention. The wing commander wants something else, and time is running out. The students ask for more information. They aren't getting it. “No, it's ambiguous for a reason because you're not always going to have what you need out there,” said retired Chief Master Sgt. Jenny Green, an instructor at Air University's Chief Leadership Academy. Green keeps the clock running. That's part of the exercise. Through the Chief Leadership Academy, Air University puts the Air Force's newest chiefs in situations where information is incomplete, priorities change and they still have to decide what comes next. “We give them a problem and, hey, go solve it,” Green said. “And then in the middle of it, hey, we're going to change it.” Sometimes that happens only minutes before students have to present. “They have to pivot very quickly,” she said. The exercise offers a look at how Air University is using the redesigned Chief Leadership Course now that the curriculum has been in place for more than a year. Instructors change conditions, limit information and bring current issues into classroom discussions to get chiefs working outside what they already know. Chief Master Sgt. Michael “Hub” Hubbard, commandant of the Chief Leadership Academy, said that's important because of the experience many students bring with them. They've spent years becoming experts in their career fields. They've generated aircraft, maintained communication networks, led medical teams, managed people and kept missions moving. Becoming a chief changes what the Air Force asks of them. “A lot of chiefs that come here, they've been in the grind,” Hubbard said. “They've been focused on the tactical level, looking down and never picking their head up.” At Air University, they're asked to pick their heads up. Before arriving at Maxwell for the in-residence portion of the course, students begin facilitated distance learning on subjects that include the National Defense Strategy and manpower. Once they're together, the conversation moves beyond their individual organizations and career fields. The goal, Hubbard said, is “a more strategic-minded leader.” That work sits inside a larger Air University mission. As an integrated enterprise, AU brings education, research, doctrine and leader development together to forge expert joint warfighters and solve operational problems for the Joint Force. The university's schools, centers, academies and other organizations contribute specialized capabilities toward those efforts. At the Chief Leadership Academy, that contribution is focused on senior enlisted professional military education. In Green's classroom, students don't always get everything they want before they're expected to act. “You can't just stop what you're doing,” she tells students when they ask for more information. “You have to figure that out.” Sometimes students have to move forward without all the information they'd like. Sometimes the solution they come up with creates another problem. Chief Master Sgt. Neel Rodgers, an academy instructor, said chiefs have to think beyond the immediate result of a decision. “As chiefs, a lot of times what our commanders come to us is to think about the second and third order effects of the decisions they're about to make,” Rodgers said. Those effects can involve readiness, resources or the Airmen expected to carry out a decision. Rodgers said instructors use the course to get students thinking about what happens beyond the immediate problem. The people sitting around the table add another part of the discussion. Air University brings active-duty, Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve leaders from different career fields, installations and operational backgrounds into the classroom. “Every class is a melting pot of experience,” Hubbard said. “All different bases, Guard, Reserve, different branches of service.” Hubbard tells students not to overlook what's already in the room. “They know more than you think they know,” he said. “You just have to talk to them.” Green saw that during a recent discussion about manpower. Guard and Reserve chiefs started explaining how their organizations handled personnel differently from the active component. Other students asked questions and compared those processes with their own experiences. “We don't always understand what Guard and Reserve does and we should be better about that,” Green said. The conversation moves beyond component lines, too. Students work through joint, interagency, intergovernmental and multinational considerations, including how they may interact with other services, government organizations, outside agencies and international partners. Green said some students initially question how much they'll use that material if they aren't headed to a traditional joint assignment. “Everything that we do across the forces is joint,” she tells them. Chiefs who've worked in those environments add their experiences to the discussion. Sometimes someone in the room has already dealt with a problem another student is seeing for the first time. “It's bigger than that,” Green said. “It's way bigger than that.” Those perspectives aren't limited to the people who come to Maxwell. Mike Wester, the academy's director of operations and a retired chief master sergeant, said the organization maintains relationships with senior enlisted education institutions in other services. Those relationships give Air University another way to bring perspectives from across the Joint Force into its enlisted education. The academy also talks with operational organizations about what they're seeing. “What are you doing on the operational front and what are the things that we're missing in our educational environments that you think our forces need to be able to operate in the joint environment?” Wester said. For Wester, those conversations help keep the course current. “As the strategic landscape changes, you have to continue to evolve and adapt to make sure that what you're providing is timely and relevant to your student population,” he said. The course itself has already gone through that kind of change. Air University paused the Chief Leadership Course for nine months while the curriculum was rebuilt. It returned in June 2025 with formal assessments and learning outcomes focused on command leadership, organizational functions and domains, strategic leadership, and joint, interagency, intergovernmental and multinational operations. The overhaul included input from major command and combatant command leaders, Air University staff, field leaders, subject matter experts and previous graduates. Hubbard said the previous curriculum wasn't giving students enough exposure to the strategic environment senior Air Force and joint leaders expected chiefs to understand. He said the redesigned course is operating at initial operating capability, and the staff continues to adjust it as requirements change. “The speed of relevance is kind of the flexibility we have within our course,” Hubbard said. That flexibility gives instructors room to bring what's happening across the force into the classroom. Green said she stays in contact with active-duty leaders and uses current examples in discussions. Students bring their own experiences with them, too. What happens in one class may not happen the same way in the next because the people in the room change. One example is a short briefing Green recently added on home station missions. Students explain what their organizations do, what they support and how their work fits into the larger mission. The briefs often lead to questions from chiefs who haven't worked around those missions. A chief who's spent a career around aircraft may know little about another student's mission. Someone from communications, medicine, security forces or another part of the Air Force may see the same problem from a different angle. Green said she wants chiefs to understand enough about the larger mission to explain it to the Airmen they lead. “What are your Airmen going to think?” she asks students. “What are you going to tell your Airmen?” “If our chiefs can understand that, then they can explain that to their Airmen,” Green said. “Their Airmen can come and say, ‘Oh, I know what my why is. I know what I'm doing, and I know why I'm doing it.’” That exchange between the operational force and the classroom is one way Air University operates as an integrated enterprise. Students bring experience and current problems into AU. Faculty draw on expertise from across the university and beyond it. Other services and operational organizations add perspectives that aren't always available within a single career field or component. Graduates then carry what they learned back to squadrons, groups, wings and staffs. The Chief Leadership Academy is one part of that larger Air University enterprise. Across AU, subordinate organizations contribute different capabilities toward the university's work to forge expert joint warfighters and solve operational problems for the Joint Force. For the academy, that starts with chiefs working beyond their functional expertise and considering problems from perspectives they may not have encountered before. Rodgers said there's a difference between reaching the Air Force's highest enlisted rank and becoming the kind of chief the course is trying to develop. “Our goal is to build chiefs, not chief master sergeant E-9 types,” he said. Green knows the classroom can't reproduce every problem they'll face once they leave. “We can't hit all the scenarios,” she said. “But we can hit a majority of them to get them thinking.” For now, the chiefs in her classroom still have a problem to solve. They don't have all the information they asked for. The situation has changed, and the solution they started with may not work anymore. Green isn't giving them anything else. They still have to figure it out.

items.title: Last produced USMC Harrier completes its final mission
items.author: Megan Wasel
items.summary: The U.S. Marine Corps’ last produced AV-8B II+ Harrier traveled to Naval Air Station Pensacola, Florida, for its final mission. BuNo 166288 was demilitarized and made safe for static display at the National Naval Aviation Museum in Pensacola.
items.body: The U.S. Marine Corps’ last produced AV-8B II+ Harrier traveled to Naval Air Station Pensacola, Florida, for its final mission this July. BuNo 166288 was demilitarized and made safe for display prior to departure by truck from Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina, and will remain on static display at the National Naval Aviation Museum in Pensacola. BuNo 166288 was delivered by Boeing in September 2003 and logged over 5,800 flight hours over the years, deploying on multiple L-Class ships and land-based sites in support of combat operations. The aircraft’s final mission and destination was organized by Pablo “Louie” Sanchez, AV-8BV/STOL Attack Program Office (PMA-257) Assistant Program Manager for Logistics (APML) and Harrier Museum Task Force Lead. Sanchez, a retired Marine Corps gunnery sergeant who has worked on the AV-8B program since 1989 as a mechanic and later a civilian within the program office, emphasized the importance of preserving the platform’s history. “Each aircraft has a story and BuNo 166288, being the last USMC-produced Harrier, seemed fitting to find its final home in the National Naval Aviation Museum,” Sanchez said. The Harrier is a single-engine, vertical/short takeoff and landing (V/STOL) ground-attack aircraft. It’s 55-year service in the U.S. Marine Corps began in 1971 with the British-built AV-8A. The platform evolved significantly in 1985 when the Marine Corps transitioned to the American-built McDonnell Douglas AV-8B Harrier II. For over four decades, the AV-8B Harrier II+ served as the cornerstone of the Marine Expeditionary Unit’s Aviation Combat Element. Operating afloat from amphibious assault ships and ashore from austere forward bases, these versatile aircraft provided vital close air support for Marines on the ground worldwide. “The arrival of the final produced AV-8B Harrier II+ at the National Naval Aviation Museum marks the end of an extraordinary chapter in Marine Corps aviation,” said Bonnie Town, National Naval Aviation Museum. “The National Naval Aviation Museum is deeply honored to preserve this historic aircraft as a lasting tribute to the extraordinary chapter of Marine Corps aviation history it represents.” In addition to residing at the museum, the aircraft’s previously removed F402-RR-408 engine will be displayed on a separate stand. The axial-flow, twin-spool turbofan engine features counter-rotating compressors and was specifically engineered to vector thrust. This revolutionary design enabled V/STOL capabilities and in-flight power nozzle breaking – a phenomenal engineering feat. Several squadrons operated the Harrier over its 55-year tenure, but Marine Attack Squadron (VMA) 223, the Bulldogs, was the last, completing the platform’s final official flight June 3. As the final Marine Corps squadron to operate the AV-8B, VMA-223 commanding officer Lt. Col. John Cumbie sees the Pensacola museum display as a permanent tribute to the entire Harrier community. “Leading this squadron through the final operational phases of the legendary AV-8B Harrier and steering our transition to the F-35B Lightning is the honor of a lifetime,” said Cumbie. “Maintaining and operating the Harrier required tireless dedication and adherence to the highest professional standards—a testament to our aviators, maintainers, and support Marines alike.” Maj. Eric Scheibe, the squadron’s executive officer, said those high professional standards were essential for managing the unique operational demands of vertical-flight technology. “The challenge of operating and maintaining the platform required a tight-knit culture of professionalism from the pilots to the maintainers and support personnel,” said Scheibe. “As we move forward to the F-35 transition, that culture and professionalism of Marine fixed-wing attack will live on in the individual Marine.” For the VMA-223 Bulldog maintainers tasked with reassembling the aircraft at NAS Pensacola, the mission is deeply personal. “After 10 years of dedication to the AV-8B Harrier platform, I am sad to see it go,” said Staff Sgt. Christian Regueira. “Working on this aircraft has been a personal blessing to me.” The transition of the AV-8B to a static museum piece is a reflective moment for the entire Harrier community, but Gunnery Sgt. Bradley Birchfield viewed the assignment as the opportunity of a lifetime. “As an AV-8B maintainer, by placing these legacy aircraft into the National Naval Aviation Museum it is the perfect end to my Harrier career,” said Birchfield. While the Harrier’s close air support chapter may be closing, the transition to fifth-generation stealth fighters ensures the future of Marine aviation remains highly lethal. The solid foundation set by the Harrier community—from development to sustainment—will support the F-35B Joint Strike Fighter program for decades of future. The F-35B replaces the AV-8B Harrier with increased sensors and speed and is increasingly effective in maintaining air dominance by delivering integrated sustainment capabilities to remain mission ready anytime, anywhere—a capability paved by decades of Harrier lessons learned.

items.title: Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Civilian Personnel Policy Michael A. Cogar Visit PNSY
items.author: Alana Demo
items.summary: PORTSMOUTH NAVAL SHIPYARD, Maine – Portsmouth Naval Shipyard and Naval Support Activity Maine (NSA Maine) welcomed Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Civilian Personnel Policy Michael A. Cogar, Sept. 9.
items.body: PORTSMOUTH NAVAL SHIPYARD, Maine – Portsmouth Naval Shipyard and Naval Support Activity Maine (NSA Maine) welcomed Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Civilian Personnel Policy Michael A. Cogar, Sept. 9. During his first visit to the shipyard since assuming his position in May 2025, Cogar engaged with shipyard leadership and subject matter experts, highlighting how the workforce processes, and emerging technologies are evolving at PNSY to meet mission-critical submarine maintenance requirements and support the Arsenal of Freedom. The visit featured a tour of Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USSWashington(SSN 787) and engagements with production and engineering teams on Model Line, a continuous improvement initiative recently implemented to aid in non-stop mechanical work. Cogar also met with subject-matter experts to discuss workforce-led innovations and advanced repair capabilities, including cold spray and additive manufacturing. “Fleet readiness is critical to our national security,” said Cogar. “The dedicated civilians of Portsmouth Naval Shipyard — both on and off the line — are essential to ensuring we remain prepared to deter and, if necessary, defeat peer adversaries. I am grateful for their expertise and unwavering commitment to the Department of War’s mission.” Portsmouth Naval Shipyard is approaching its workforce, processes, and resources with a focus on aligning civilian talent to mission-critical needs. This effort builds on PNSY’s legacy and our gold-standard performance set by our shipyard workforce, ensuring our work aligns with the Department of War readiness priorities and warfighter needs. “Deputy Secretary Cogar’s visit gave us the opportunity to showcase the people, partnerships, and capabilities that enable Portsmouth Naval Shipyard to deliver for the fleet,” said Capt. Jesse Nice, shipyard commander. “Our workforce is finding better ways to execute critical maintenance through their expertise and commitment, and these efforts are already producing tangible results across the shipyard — some of which we had the pleasure of sharing with DASW Cogar today.” As America’s leader for attack submarine maintenance, repair, and modernization, Portsmouth Naval Shipyard delivers the decisive edge required to master an era of evolving threats. It stands at the forefront of America's commitment to peace through strength, delivering combat-ready submarines that are lethal, resilient, and prepared to win. The work performed at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard directly contributes to national security, ensuring the U.S. Navy remains the most dominant maritime force anywhere in the world.

items.title: Five years later, Afghan guests return to Fort McCoy that became part of their journey
items.author: Scott Sturkol
items.summary: When several young Afghan women arrived at Fort McCoy on Aug. 19, they were no longer the teenagers who had stepped off buses here five years earlier.
items.body:
When several young Afghan women arrived at Fort McCoy on Aug. 19, they were no longer the teenagers who had stepped off buses here five years earlier.

They were now young women in their early 20s, college students living in another state, and building lives in a new country. But as they pulled up to one particular brick building at Fort McCoy, something from their past came rushing back.

“The energy in the car totally changed,” said Jane Donaldson, a Tomah, Wis., business owner who accompanied the women on their return visit. “Because that’s like a very distinct memory for them.”

The building was part of the Fort McCoy facilities where the young women had lived during Operation Allies Welcome, the six-month humanitarian mission that brought approximately 12,600 Afghan guests to Fort McCoy beginning Aug. 22, 2021.

Five years after their arrival, several women had returned to the installation for the first time. Their visit offered something unusual — a chance for people who experienced Operation Allies Welcome as teenagers to see Fort McCoy again as adults — and to see a place that once represented uncertainty and transition from an entirely different perspective.

“It perhaps gave some closure to that particular time, just to see it again,” Donaldson said. “You know how when you go back and see something … it gives you a newer perspective.”

From Afghanistan to Wisconsin

The women were among thousands of Afghans evacuated from their country in 2021 as part of Operation Allies Welcome. According to the Feb. 25, 2022, end-of-mission report by the Fort McCoy Public Affairs Office, Fort McCoy began receiving Afghan guests Aug. 22, 2021, and ultimately supported approximately 12,600 people during the mission. More than 4,000 people representing 35 federal, state, local, non-governmental, and volunteer organizations participated in the operation.

The women who returned to Fort McCoy in August 2026 were teenagers when they lived here. Donaldson said the women came from Afghanistan’s Bamyan region, an area she described as having a particularly difficult history for women and girls.

“They’re in their early 20s,” Donaldson said. “So, they were babies or born … after we started building back the government. So, they had a very different experience than their mothers who were there during the height of Taliban.”

Donaldson said that experience shaped the young women and their hopes for the future.

“These young women … are so much the hope for Afghanistan,” she said.

The women eventually received scholarships and continued their education at universities in the United States. Donaldson said other young women from the same group went to colleges in several states.

For two of the three who returned to Fort McCoy, however, their connection to the place where their American journey began remained.

A connection that began during OAW

Donaldson’s involvement with the Afghan guests began during the operation. She said she traveled to Fort McCoy once or twice a week for the duration of the mission, working with women and children at one of the community centers established throughout the temporary Afghan guest area.

It was there that Donaldson developed relationships with several young women. One woman became an important connection. Donaldson described her as a “fabulous interpreter” who also served as a leader among the women.

Donaldson said the group included approximately 144 women who had been sponsored by the Cindy McCain Humanitarian Initiative. Her involvement with Afghanistan also predated Operation Allies Welcome by nearly two decades.

Donaldson said she traveled to Afghanistan in 2003 while living in France and worked with a French-Afghan group during the constitutional convention process.

She later returned to Boston University for three months to study international public health and said that, because of her experience in Afghanistan, she frequently focused on the country during her studies.

Later, while living in Paris, Donaldson said she helped host 30 of Afghanistan’s 69 female parliamentarians for a week, taking them to the French Senate and National Assembly. Those experiences gave Donaldson a longstanding connection to Afghanistan and its people.

That connection took on a new meaning when thousands of Afghans arrived at Fort McCoy in 2021.

When a military installation became home

For the Afghan guests, Fort McCoy was never intended to be a permanent home. It was a staging and processing location while they waited for documentation, family connections, and resettlement opportunities.

Donaldson said that distinction is important when people today ask what happened to the approximately 13,000 Afghans who were at Fort McCoy.

“They are everywhere,” Donaldson said.

She explained that some people stayed only a few weeks while others remained for most or all the six-month operation.

“A lot of these folks … had connections in the U.S.,” Donaldson said. “And they were just waiting for those people to connect with them and get their visas done. And then they were out of here.”

The Fort McCoy Public Affairs Office reported in February 2022 that the final Afghan guests departed the installation Feb. 15, 2022. But Donaldson's connection with some of the young women did not end when they left.

She continued communicating with several of them, occasionally talking with them by phone and maintaining connections with others who had also become involved with the women during their time at Fort McCoy.

A community reaches out

Donaldson said the connection between the Afghan guests and people in the surrounding communities became one of the most memorable parts of the OAW experience. She emphasized that she was far from the only person who became involved.

“It’s not just me,” Donaldson said. “There were several people that really connected with these young women.”

Tomah residents organized efforts to make the women feel welcome. Donaldson recalled a project in which women from Tomah assembled makeup bags for Afghan women and girls. Some people questioned whether makeup was an important thing to provide during such a massive humanitarian operation.

But Donaldson said the response from the women showed otherwise.

“When they gave out the makeup, it was so exciting for them,” she said. “I don’t know, it made them feel good about themselves.”

She said the effort was one of many examples of people in Tomah looking for ways to make the Afghan guests feel welcome.

“There are just some phenomenal women in Tomah,” Donaldson said.

The effort also reflected a larger community response to the mission.

According to the Fort McCoy’s end-of-mission reporting, local organizations, churches, businesses, volunteers and other community groups provided assistance and donations during the operation.

A difficult beginning

Donaldson remembers that the early days of OAW were chaotic. She said she was working approximately 12-hour days during the first week or so of the operation, often answering phone calls from people wanting to donate clothing and other supplies.

“I was a suitcase lady at the end of the day,” Donaldson said, recalling the hundreds of suitcases and other items involved in the effort.

The early response also included people trying to figure out how they could help.

Donaldson recalled seeing a large truckload of watermelons at the Tomah farmers market and wondering how the fruit could be delivered to Fort McCoy. She also worked with the armory in Sparta, Wis., which accepted some donated items.

Inside Fort McCoy, meanwhile, personnel were building the infrastructure needed to support thousands of people who had arrived with very little.

Donaldson recalled that many of the Afghan guests had left their country with virtually nothing.

“All of the 13,000 of them left their country with nothing,” she said. “They just loaded on a plane and left.”

News reports from the time document the enormous scale of the response, including food, medical care, education, recreation, and other support. The installation ultimately provided approximately 87,000 vaccinations, established 12 informal schools conducting approximately 70 classes per day, and helped connect more than 100 female Afghan university students with scholarship opportunities.

Seeing Fort McCoy again

The women did not initially return to Wisconsin specifically to revisit Fort McCoy. Donaldson said two of the women were coming to the Minneapolis area because a cousin was getting married.

They flew into Minneapolis and then traveled to Tomah to visit Donaldson and others who had become friends with them. Donaldson asked whether they wanted to return to Fort McCoy. They did.

The process of arranging the visit was much easier than she expected. Donaldson said she was unsure what paperwork the women might need and wondered whom she could contact at Fort McCoy. But the visit came together quickly.

“They had the plan to come up to … Minneapolis,” Donaldson said. “So, they decided to come. They flew into Minneapolis and then they drove down to Tomah to see us. And to go toward the base.”

Once they arrived at Fort McCoy, Donaldson said the women were fascinated by the installation’s history as they went through the Fort McCoy History Center and the Fort McCoy Commemorative Area. But their strongest reaction came when they reached the brick building where they had lived as teenagers.

“When we pulled up to the building, the brick building, the energy in the car totally changed,” Donaldson said.

The women did not go inside, but Donaldson said simply seeing the building was emotional for them.

“They were fascinated with the history of it,” she said. “It was emotional.”

For Donaldson, the reaction illustrated how much the experience had stayed with them. Five years earlier, the building had been part of an unfamiliar military installation where they had arrived after an extraordinary journey from Afghanistan.

Now they were returning as college students.

A day beyond the gates

The return visit did not end at the Fort McCoy building. Donaldson said the women also spent time exploring the area, stopping for ice cream in Baraboo, Wis., and later taking a boat ride on the Mississippi River.

The river trip became one of the highlights of the day.

“It was a riot,” Donaldson said. “It was just so much fun.”

The women saw bald eagles and experienced the Mississippi River from a friend’s boat. For women who had once lived inside a restricted portion of Fort McCoy and had little opportunity to see the world immediately outside the installation, the day offered a dramatically different experience.

Donaldson said that when the women first lived at Fort McCoy, they often did not know where they were.

“They really didn’t see outside of their restricted area on base,” she said.

She recalled that many guests arrived and departed by bus, sometimes at night or while they were sleeping.

“So, who knows what they actually saw,” Donaldson said.

Their return was different. This time, they were not arriving as evacuees. They were visitors. They were able to see Fort McCoy, visit with people who had helped them and experience some of the surrounding region.

And they were able to return to a place that had been an important stop in their journey.

Five years, a different perspective

Operation Allies Welcome ended at Fort McCoy in February 2022. History shows that the final guests had departed and that the installation’s six-month humanitarian mission had concluded. Five years later, the mission has become part of Fort McCoy’s history.

The installation now preserves that history through its Fort McCoy History Center, where an Operation Allies Welcome exhibit helps tell the story of the people who lived and worked here during the operation.

For Donaldson, however, OAW has never simply been history. It remains connected to people she knows. She continues to communicate with several of the young women. She said another friend has traveled to Arizona to visit some of them, while one of the young women has traveled to New York to visit a friend’s daughter.

Their lives have spread across the country. Their families, however, remain a long distance away. Donaldson said the women’s mothers and sisters remain in Afghanistan, and she hopes that one day they will be able to join them in the United States.

For now, the women who returned Aug. 19 were able to revisit one small but significant part of their journey. Donaldson described Fort McCoy as “a brief respite on their journey.”

But five years later, the visit showed that the brief stop had left a lasting impression.

“I think for a lot of people to get exposed to their culture, it was” meaningful, Donaldson said.

The experience worked both ways. The Afghan guests encountered a part of America they had never expected to see. The people of Fort McCoy and the surrounding communities encountered young women whose lives had been dramatically altered by events thousands of miles away. And some of those connections lasted long after the buses left Fort McCoy.

As the women stood outside the brick building where they once lived, they were no longer simply Afghan guests awaiting the next step in an uncertain journey. They were college students. They were young women building new lives. And for a few hours, they were visitors returning to a place that had once been temporary — but had become part of their story.

For Donaldson, that was perhaps the most meaningful part of the visit.

“It was good for them,” she said. “It perhaps gave some closure to that particular time.”

Five years after Operation Allies Welcome began at Fort McCoy, the mission’s statistics remain impressive. But the return of these women offers another way to understand what happened here in 2021 and 2022. The mission lasted six months. The memories lasted much longer.

items.body: Who is U.S. Army Capt. Latoiya Templeton?That’sa question evenshestruggled to answer. “Ohgosh, I am so many things, I am a mom,I’ma veterinarian,I’ma sister,I’madaughter. All the things,”said Templeton,Joint Base Andrews branch chiefassigned to the Veterinary Readiness Activity, Fort Belvoir. Templeton grew upon the south side ofChicagoto17-year-old parents. Itwasn’tan easy life growing up, she described her early childhood as a community effort to raiseher andhersiblings.But it was thoseformative years thatpointed her toward her true calling.Her parents and grandparents,including a grandfather who enlisted in the U.S.Army in 1958,paved the way with a simple message:“There’s nothing you can’t do.” “The thing I saw growing up was so much need,”said Templeton.“It wasvery importantto me, whatever my purpose was,would be giving back,in which ever way I was most effective.” And that was as a veterinarian. A few weeks before herthirdyear of veterinarian school, Templeton gave birth toher daughter, Kennedy.Describing that as one ofherdefining moments inlife, veterinary school and a newborn was an unthinkable challenge.Templetonwas given theoptionto delayher schooling bya year ortocontinuejuggling classes andabrand-newdaughter.Shechose tocontinuewith her classestograduate on time. “Everybody helped out, even with the little things,”said Templeton. “They left it up to me, to write my own path and I knew I could bet on myself.” Herprofessorswereveryhelpful,allowingtheir classes to be didactic,whichmeantthatshe wasableto sit at home andlisten to lectures,one ofthe first timethis wasallowedattheOhio State University. “I thinkthat’swhy I advocate so hard for the dogs,because a lot of timeswe’redoingthings one way, butthat’snot the only way to do it,”said Templeton.She emphasized that someone must be brave enough to voice an alternative and dedicated enough to run with the vision. Capt. Templeton arrived at Joint Base Andrews inDecember2025 butdidn’tfully take over as theBranch ChiefatJBAuntil April2026.Responsibility forthe largestoperationalMWD kennel in the Air Force with 36 dogswas daunting for Templeton, but thatdidn’tdeter herfrom tackling the challenge. “If I can have a kid in vet school, if Iif I can direct commissioninto the U.S.Army Veterinary Corps atage38... it reminds methatI can do this too,”she said. The same monthTempleton officiallytook over,Department ofAirForceInstruction31-126DoDMilitary Working Dog Program, was republished with guidance coveringMWD health and welfare,animal welfare principles,companion animal care guidelines,kennel managementprinciplesand procedures,andaMWD enrichment policy. Since stepping into her role as the new Branch Chief of Joint Base Andrews, Templeton hasbrought in a wave of newinnovations on existing processes. She also started a few of her own, including celebrating each of her assigned MWDs on their birthdays. Every day,one thing alwaysremainstop of mind regarding MWDs for Templeton:readiness. “The Andrews kennelis always our busiest kennel,”Templeton said.Because this is a presidential base, the mission takes precedence whenever these dogs are operational, including conducting security sweeps for Air Force One and Air Force Two. Making sure the MWDs areready to complete their no-fail mission, Templeton and her team make monthly visits to the kennelfor their “K9readiness evaluation day.”On thosedays,all the MWDs are evaluatedfornewhealth concernsand receive targeted physical exams for travel certifications. The kennel facilities are inspected, and Templeton’s team conducts medical training.Sheand her teamtrainthe handlers onbest practicesforhealth and readiness evaluations, hot andcold weatherinjuries,CanineTactical Combat Casualty Care, and a variety of other topics.According to DAFI 31-126the handlersare responsible forgrooming,dailyhealthand well-being evaluations,andemergency medicalcare. Templeton isthrilledwith how the dogs are being cared for under the new DAFI. “The things that we didn’t think about as a military beforehand are now at the forefront,” she said. “These (dogs) arecategorized asmilitary equipment,”Templetonsaid. “But when you see them work,you’rejust in awebecausethey aremagical. Theyare so motivated to work, despite all the environmental challenges.” It’s that daily buy-in from the dogswho never chose toserve butwere born into it and selected by the military,that has made Templeton so committed to providing them with the highest level of care possible for as long as they’re in service. “I do this because no one can do it better than me formydogs, because Igenuinelylove it,”Templeton said.“Ilove my job, andI think itgives back in a way that makes you feel like a better human.” Whetherit means caring for the dogs through their daily antics or simply letting them be dogs, for Capt. Templeton, the work is a rewarding way to serve and set a meaningful example for her two children. “Being a good person is just the baseline—the minimum standard we should all live by,” Templeton said with a smile. “Being able to support this mission means serving something greater than myself. Pouring that energy back into the world, and into these dogs, is what brings everything full circle.”

items.title: Hypersonic Aircraft Startup Adding Anduril’s Autonomy Software for 2027 Flight
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force. The post Hypersonic Aircraft Startup Adding Anduril’s Autonomy Software for 2027 Flight appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Startups Anduril Industries and Heremus have agreed to integrate Anduril’s autonomy software onto Hermeus’ hypersonic demonstrator aircraft “Quarterhorse”—uniting two technologies that have drawn keen interest and investment from the Air Force.

The firms announced the deal Sept. 3 and said they plan to fly the Quarterhorse Mk 2 aircraft using the Lattice autonomy system in 2027.

Hermeus is attempting to build a reusable aircraft that can reach hypersonic speeds, defined as Mach 5 and above, and has received funding and support from the Air Force. Quarterhorse has yet to go that fast—company officials say they’re targeting supersonic speeds, or Mach 1-plus, as the next step in their test campaign—but adding autonomy software could enable faster control of the aircraft as it flies around a mile per second.

At the same time, preparing the software for the platform will take time.

“We will spend the rest of this year on a build-up from software in the loop to integration testing to hardware in the loop and validation testing, then we’ll go toward flight,” Brett Darcey, vice president for mission autonomy at Anduril, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Anduril is already refining its autonomy software, dubbed Lattice, for the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. The firm is competing with Shield AI and Collins Aerospace on that front. Anduril is also building its FQ-44A Fury drone as one of the CCA airframes, along with General Atomics’ FQ-42A Dark Merlin.

But while Anduril has experience with the CCA program, CCAs aren’t meant to be supersonic nor hypersonic like Quarterhorse. The speeds at which that aircraft will operate will require beyond human-like decision-making speeds. The Autonomy Government Reference Architecture that serves as the baseline for most contractor’s autonomy software requires that Quarterhorse be able to fly itself “through all regimes of flight, which would include the jump to supersonic,” Darcey said.

That means human operators will tell the software to fly at a certain velocity, and the software will be responsible for taking the steps to execute the command.

“That probably means we’re going to do a lot of software and hardware in the loop testing, and a lot of independent validation of what we are doing on the route generation side, and appropriately, I think the monitoring of execution of those routes when we’re at those high speeds on the build-up phase all the way to flight,” Darcey said.

That step-by-step approach is necessary as companies work to build trust in the software’s ability to control the aircraft’s flight and other taskings for its human operators.

Tactics, techniques, and procedures are still developing and evolving to build that trust between human and machine, but Darcey was quick to note that in the development stage there can be too little trust; at times, there can also be too much.

He likens it to using an actual horse in warfare. Horses are independent, thinking creatures that can also be trained to do certain things. Cavalrymen would build their trust in the “human-horse system” over time, instead of just jumping on a horse and going to war.

A key difference between autonomy software and an actual horse, though, is that the software has built-in debrief functions that will tell the user what it did and why. And as developers of the software, sharing that data with their company partners and the Air Force provides transparency for the process, Darcey said.

CCA and Mission Autonomy

In February , Anduril’s developmental YFQ-44A flew with two different mission autonomy software suites on the same aircraft during the same flight, using both Lattice and Shield AI’s Hivemind suite.

“We do have an advantage with Fury,” Darcey said. “That kind of deep platform knowledge definitely is useful.”

But Darcey was quick to point out that the company isn’t tying all its software thinking to its own platform, or even to a single platform. The software used in the CCA program must also be viable for a wide range of aircraft types, based on USAF requirements.

“One of the big challenges with mission autonomy is it has to be generally built so it can do the mission requirements of multiple platforms at once,” Darcey said.

Quarterhorse

Hermeus conducted its first flight with the Mk1 model in May 2025 and then flew its Mk 2.1 demonstration vehicle in another flight in March.

That flight ran from Spaceport America past White Sands Missile Range, N.M., with operators piloting the aircraft from a ground-based flight deck, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.

The Mk 2 aircraft is roughly the size of an F-16 fighter.

The company won a $1.5 million contract in 2020 for a future hypersonic Presidential and Executive Airlift fleet via AFWERX, an Air Force innovation arm within the Air Force Research Laboratory.

In 2021, Hermeus won a $60 million Strategic Funding Increase contract via AFWERX and the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center

The Defense Innovation Unit awarded Hermeus a $23 million contract in 2023 for technologies related to the unit’s larger goal of creating a Hypersonic High-Cadence Airborne Testing Capabilities program.

items.title: Building Readiness Through Relationships
items.author: Wesley Burgos
items.summary: Readiness can start long before a ship gets underway or an aircraft launch. Sometimes it starts with a conversation and a relationship built before there is a problem to solve. At NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor’s Joint Personal Property Shipping Office (JPPSO) Hawaii, those relationships are put to work every day.
items.body:
PEARL HARBOR, Hawaii — Readiness can start long before a ship gets underway or an aircraft launch. Sometimes it starts with a conversation and a relationship built before there is a problem to solve.

At NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor’s Joint Personal Property Shipping Office (JPPSO) Hawaii, those relationships are put to work every day.

From May through August 2026, the JPPSO Hawaii Personal Property Department submitted 1,630 shipment applications for booking, supporting service members and families moving to and from Hawaii. During the same period, the Shipment Management Department booked 4,456 shipments.

As the office comes out of the annual peak permanent change of station season, JPPSO Hawaii is taking stock of one of its busiest periods of the year. The office coordinates the movement of household goods for service members and families from the Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps and Coast Guard moving to and from Hawaii.

The work brings together military personnel, transportation companies, carriers and local moving agents across multiple organizations and locations. During peak season, when move volume increases and time is limited, established relationships can make the difference between waiting for an answer and finding a solution.

“During peak season, the most important relationship is the one we have within our JPPSO team. The demands can be challenging, and there will always be moments of stress or disagreement, but what matters is how we support one another and work through those challenges together. We communicate, resolve conflicts, share the most current information, and make sure no one feels like they are carrying the workload alone,” said Joanne Lilo, transportation officer, JPPSO Hawaii.

At JPPSO Hawaii, that teamwork is part of how the office approaches its mission.

“At JPPSO Hawai‘i, ‘Ohana is more than just a word, it is who we are. It means looking out for one another, stepping in when someone needs help, celebrating each other’s successes, and getting through the difficult days together. We may not always agree, but at the end of the day, we are one team, one ‘Ohana, working toward the same mission,” Lilo said.

For Nicole Gumban, personal property supervisor, JPPSO Hawaii, strong relationships also provide a practical advantage when service members need answers quickly.

“Relationships or the lack can either help or hinder when you are in a moment of crunch,” Gumban said. “I’ve been with NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor JPPSO Personal Property for seven years. I spent the first five years as an entitlements counselor and have been a supervisor for the past two years. During that time, I’ve learned that who you know matters when you’re looking for an answer for a service member sitting in front of you.”

During peak season, the office often has little time to find answers to complex problems.

“We often need immediate solutions to complex problems, and the relationships we’ve built over time can be a major factor in how successfully we resolve those challenges,” Gumban said.

For Capt. Anthony P. Bannister, commanding officer, NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor, that ability to communicate and solve problems is directly connected to readiness.

“Readiness starts with relationships,” Bannister said. “Talking with people creates awareness of possible logistical solutions and provides a deeper understanding of what our customers need to accomplish their missions. By strengthening relationships with our customers, we enable meaningful discussions and proper planning before challenges occur. When the team is faced with challenges, those relationships ensure we are ready, aligned and prepared to execute.”

Those relationships extend beyond the office and into Hawaii’s local transportation industry.

Moving household goods to or from Hawaii is more than a change of address. It can involve transportation by land, sea and air, multiple organizations and coordination across thousands of miles. JPPSO Hawaii works with transportation service providers and carriers as well as 10 local moving agents that support household goods shipments on the island.

“Coming through peak PCS season really reinforced for me how important our relationships with our local transportation partners are,” Lilo said. “When an issue comes up, we can pick up the phone and communicate directly with someone here on island who understands our environment and the challenges we face.”

That local connection can be especially valuable when a military family needs help quickly.

One situation during this year’s peak season showed what that relationship can accomplish.

A service member and spouse contacted JPPSO because they were concerned that not enough time was being spent at their residence and worried their move would not be completed on schedule.

As JPPSO already had an established relationship with the local moving company, the team was able to communicate directly with the company and discuss the family’s concerns.

“Although the company was operating within requirements, they adjusted their schedule and sent a full crew the next day, including their general manager, who personally assisted with the packing,” Lilo said. “Having management out in the field during peak season demonstrates a company’s attention to going above and beyond for customer service.”

By the third day, the situation had changed.

“The member contacted our quality assurance office and said an inspector was no longer necessary because the move was going smoothly,” Lilo said. “For me, that was a great example of what a strong working relationship can accomplish. The company wasn’t required to make those additional adjustments, but they understood the concern and worked with us to take care of the family.”

For military families, a moving issue is more than a delay in packing schedule. It is one more uncertainty during a major life transition.

That interaction represents only one part of a much larger process.

“I wish our customers had a better understanding of what really goes into making a move happen,” Gumban said. “What they see is just a small piece of a much larger logistical puzzle that has to come together to get their household goods from one geographic location to another.”

The scale of that effort is reflected in the numbers. From May through August, JPPSO Hawaii conducted 9,508 quality assurance inspections and processed 16,979 invoices totaling more than $132.3 million.

During the same period, 4,145 customers received 5,177 inbound shipments containing more than 20.2 million pounds of personal property. For outbound moves, 5,187 customers had 6,240 shipments picked up, totaling more than 27.7 million pounds of personal property.

“There are a lot of complex issues we work through every day, and our geographic location adds another layer of challenges,” Gumban said. “Operating in Hawaii with a limited number of government approved transportation providers and available warehouse storage space can create challenges and frustration when families are waiting for their household goods to be picked up or delivered.”

“There are a lot of people working behind the scenes to make each move happen, and sometimes the challenges we are working through are not visible to the family.”

Those challenges are not confined to the office.

JPPSO quality assurance specialists travel throughout Oahu to inspect household goods pickups and deliveries at service members’ residences. Their work puts them alongside transportation representatives during critical points in the moving process, where direct communication can help address concerns and identify issues before they become larger problems.

Household goods moving between Hawaii and the continental United States can involve multiple transportation requirements and organizations, making coordination essential from pickup through delivery.

When capacity is limited, those relationships become even more important.

“There are times when capacity is extremely limited or companies are already fully booked, but we may receive a priority or short notice requirement that still needs support,” Lilo said. “Having established relationships gives us the ability to communicate directly with our partners, explain the situation and see what can be done to fully support the mission.”

That relationship works both ways.

“We provide guidance and support to our industry partners to help them understand requirements and maintain compliance, and they work with us to meet the needs of our military families,” Lilo said. “Ultimately, we are all part of the same network, and maintaining those relationships helps us support our customers while contributing to Navy and joint force readiness.”

The connection between household goods and readiness may not be obvious, but it becomes clear from the perspective of the service member preparing for the next assignment.

“I absolutely see household goods as part of the readiness mission,” Lilo said. “When service members know their families and personal property are being taken care of, it allows them to focus on their next assignment and the mission ahead.”

Readiness is forged through communication, coordination and relationships built before a challenge becomes a crisis. Peak PCS season puts those relationships to the test, but their value extends well beyond the busiest months of the year.

At NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor and JPPSO Hawaii, readiness starts with relationships and service is delivered with aloha.

As one of 11 commands within the NAVSUP Enterprise, NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor enables forward operations and sustains fleet readiness throughout the Indo-Pacific. Naval Supply Systems Command provides supply, acquisition and logistics support to the Navy and joint force worldwide. Headquartered in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, NAVSUP employs military and civilian personnel across the globe. Together, NAVSUP and the Navy Supply Corps conduct and enable global supply chain management, acquisition, operational logistics, and Sailor and family services in partnership with the fleet to generate readiness and sustain naval forces.

items.title: UK Armed Forces pay tribute to late King of Norway at his funeral in Oslo
items.summary: Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.
items.body:
Royal Marines and British Army personnel attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday.

20 Royal Marines provided a marching detachment lining the route of the funeral procession in Oslo. Personnel from 1st Battalion, The Yorkshire Regiment, also attended as part of the UK’s tribute.

The late King, who died on 28 August, maintained a dedicated 45-year relationship with the British Armed Forces as an Honorary Colonel in the UK Royal Marines and an Honorary General in the British Army. He met with UK Commando Forces leadership every year and maintained a sharp, active interest in the Corps.

King Harald V’s father, King Olav V, was appointed an Honorary Admiral in the Royal Navy in 1958. In 1961, he and his son, the then Crown Prince Harald, were hosted onboard the Royal Navy aircraft carrier HMS Hermes during her regional engagement visit to Oslo.

The then Crown Prince Harald was appointed Honorary Colonel of the Royal Marines in March 1981 by Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the first such appointment involving a member of a foreign Royal household in the Corps’ history. He paid his first visit to the Royal Marines that October, touring CTCRM Lympstone and RM Bickleigh, where he watched a cliff assault by 40 Commando and a demonstration of jungle warfare training by 42 Commando.

His connection with the Royal Marines continued throughout his reign. In 2018, he visited Royal Marines from X Company, 45 Commando, at Vaernes Camp in Norway during Exercise Trident Juncture, NATO’s largest collective defence exercise in a decade, where he was briefed on the Corps’ role in the exercise and joined celebrations marking the Royal Marines’ 354th birthday.

items.title: Saab tapped to continue work on Sweden’s next flagship fighter jet
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: The Swedish government has tapped Saab to continue work on a next-generation fighter jet concept, keeping a wholly domestic iron in the fire.
items.body:
Europe

Saab tapped to continue work on Sweden’s next flagship fighter jet

A Saab JAS-39E Gripen performs at the Flight Days 2026 event in Malmen, Linkoping, Sweden, on Aug. 22, 2026. (Pradeep Dambarage/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

VIENNA — Saab has received a new contract worth approximately SEK 2.9 billion (roughly $303 million) from Sweden’s Defense Materiel Administration, FMV, to continue conceptual work on the country’s future fighter system, the company announced in a statement Wednesday.

The deal’s work period runs from 2026 to 2028, with options extending into 2029 and 2030, and builds on agreements signed in 2024 and 2025.

According to Saab, the work covers flying and ground-based demonstrators, advanced studies and the development of future system concepts for both manned and unmanned platforms. The company says the program is meant to strengthen Sweden’s capabilities in systems integration, autonomy, signature adaptation, propulsion and digital development, while reducing technical risk and preserving “freedom of action” for future decisions on the country’s air combat capability.

Lars Tossman, head of Saab’s Aeronautics business area, said in the statement that FMV’s continued confidence in Saab is “crucial to further develop and demonstrate new technologies that will be central to future fighter system.”

The order is the third in a series of awards tied to Sweden’s Koncept för Framtida Stridsflyg (KFS) program, also referred to as Vägval stridsflyg, which is intended to shape the country’s air power beyond 2040. The initial contract was signed in March 2024, followed by a SEK 2.6 billion extension in October 2025 covering 2025 to 2027. That earlier phase included plans for a flying demonstrator, with concept and technology development originally set to wrap up by the third quarter of 2026 and initial flight tests to follow in 2027.

Saab has previously outlined a family of concepts under its F-series branding, including a crewed fighter alongside subsonic and supersonic uncrewed platforms of varying weight classes and form factors.

The KFS was launched after Sweden withdrew from the British-led Team Tempest project, which would later become GCAP, in 2023, opting instead for its own domestic development.

Saab plays a crucial role in Sweden as the country’s only manufacturer of fighter jets, and its aircraft have made up the backbone of the Swedish air force for decades. Currently, the Saab Gripen plays this role.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: Iran and US hit tankers in biggest wave of attacks on shipping since war began
items.author: Enas Alashray, Idrees Ali and Jana Choukeir, Reuters
items.summary: Recent attacks by the U.S. and Iran have shattered a month of relative calm, with both hitting military, shipping and energy assets.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Iran and US hit tankers in biggest wave of attacks on shipping since war began

Iranian crude oil carriers after being struck. U.S. Central Command says it targeted the carriers after attempted Iranian missile attacks on a U.S. Navy warship over the past two days. (U.S. Central Command via Reuters)

Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war.

At least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed and another listed as missing. The attacks sent the price of oil surging, with the international Brent crude benchmark breaching $100 a barrel for the first time since July.

Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the U.S. and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets.

The Revolutionary Guards said they would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, and if the enemy struck two or three Iranian targets, Iran would respond by hitting 20. Iran would soon release maps of a new, much larger off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as the Arabian Gulf off Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran’s coast near Pakistan, the Guards said.

Recent days have also seen an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East.

Video shows Iranian tankers ablaze

The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The U.S. military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a U.S. Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the U.S. said.

Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships. Iran says it is using new, more capable missiles to attack U.S. ships.

“Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia.

After Iran announced its strikes in response, saying it fired on two U.S. ships and eight tankers, reports indicated vessels had been hit in waters near several neighbouring countries.

One seafarer was killed aboard the oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage off Dubai and another crew member was missing, the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula, said. Maritime security sources said it may have been hit by a drone.

The British maritime security agency UKMTO described a vessel in the vicinity that was listing, possibly taking on water after being struck by a projectile. Reuters could not immediately determine whether this referred to the same ship. Two Iraqi port officials said a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of fuel oil, the New Andros, had caught fire after being struck by a drone in Iraqi waters. There were no reports of casualties among the 22 crew.

The UKMTO said it had received reports of several merchant ships struck by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman, on either side of the strait. It was not immediately able to confirm casualties or environmental impact.

Iran also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan.

The IRGC also said on Wednesday it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by U.S. forces near Al Azraq, in eastern Jordan. Jordan said its air defences had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas and no casualties. A U.S. official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for.

Video filmed in Ash-Shajarah, in northern Jordan, and verified by Reuters showed flashes lighting up the night sky.

Strait choked off

Iran has largely choked off transit through the strait that carried a fifth of global oil before the war.

Washington has responded with a blockade of Iranian ports, and says it has been able to guide many tankers through the strait, although independent monitors say the extent to which oil is escaping has become increasingly difficult to assess. Preliminary data showed just six ships crossing with transponders on over the last 24 hours.

Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement that controls most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets. A Saudi-backed government based in the south of Yemen has launched a multi-pronged assault on areas controlled by the Houthis, who have threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

On Tuesday, the Houthis launched an attack on four cities in Saudi Arabia, causing huge fires at oil installations that were visible from space. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded. The Saudi Press Agency released footage showing homes severely damaged and injured patients in hospital.

A source in Pakistan, which signed a mutual defence pact with Riyadh last month, said Saudi Arabia had carried out retaliatory strikes on Yemen. The Houthis say dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed.

items.body:
Military low flying: RAF operational low flying training timetable

Royal Air Force (RAF) operational low flying training timetables in 3 areas of the UK.

From:

Ministry of Defence

Published:

1 August 2011

Last updated:

9 September 2026 — See all updates

Documents

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 7 to 11 September 2026

HTML

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 14 to 18 September 2026

Operational Low Flying Training Timetable 21 September to 25 September 2026

Details

Timetables for operational low flying ( OLF ) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas ( TTA ) only. These are:

LFA 7(T): central Wales

LFA 14(T): northern Scotland

LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England

When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.

Other low flying schedules

Military low flying: MOD sponsored air exercises

Military low flying: air weapons ranges activity

Related information

Low flying military aircraft includes information about how to contact MOD about low flying in your area

Military low flying includes detailed information about why we carry out low flying in the UK
