items.title: What Can Public Data Tell Us About Corporate Support for Veterans?
items.author: Jeffrey B. Wenger
items.summary: The authors analyzed public disclosures, foundation tax returns, and federal contractor reports to assess how S&P 500 companies support veterans and found little alignment among corporate statements, foundation giving, and protected veteran hiring.
items.body:
The authors analyzed public disclosures, foundation tax returns, federal contractor reports, and interviews to assess how S&P 500 companies support veterans. Corporate statements, foundation giving, and protected veteran hiring showed little alignment. Public data also revealed far more about hiring than about retention or advancement. The report provides targeted improvements to disclosure and contractor-reporting systems.

What Can Public Data Tell Us About Corporate Support for Veterans?

George Zuo , Jeffrey B. Wenger

Research Published Sep 9, 2026

Includes Annex, S&P 500 Corporate Veteran Support Scorecard

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Major U.S. corporations frequently make visible commitments to hiring and supporting veterans, yet limited evidence shows whether those commitments translate into sustained employment, advancement, or financial investment. The authors examined the gap between corporate statements and observable action by comparing public disclosures, philanthropic giving, federal contractor employment reports, and qualitative evidence. The authors focused on Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500) companies because they include many of the country’s largest employers, most visible corporate brands, and major federal contractors, making them a natural test case for corporate accountability to veterans.

The authors’ findings reveal weak alignment among corporate statements, foundation giving, and publicly reported protected veteran hiring. Many large companies describe veteran initiatives in voluntary reports, websites, and press releases, yet most offer little or no veteran‑related information in mandatory Securities and Exchange Commission filings. Across these sources, what companies say, what they give, and who they hire often diverge in meaningful ways.

This fragmented data infrastructure limits accountability. Policymakers, investors, procurement officials, veteran advocates, and corporate leaders lack a consistent basis for assessing how corporate commitments align with observable hiring and financial investment. Much of the usable information comes from web-scraped text disclosures, and existing data collection mandates reveal virtually nothing about job outcomes beyond workforce snapshots and new-hire counts for federal contractors. The report provides practical policy recommendations to improve transparency and accountability, with a focus on established but underutilized regulatory and statutory channels.

Key Takeaways

What companies say about veteran support only weakly aligns with how they give and hire. Companies with stronger veteran disclosures do not consistently direct more foundation giving to veteran causes or report higher protected veteran hiring rates.

Voluntary corporate communications contain far more detail about veteran efforts than mandatory filings to investors do. Firms often describe veteran initiatives on websites, corporate social responsibility reports, and press releases, but most firms say little or nothing in investor-facing annual filings.

The broader diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) retreat may have spilled over to veteran programs. High-quality regulatory disclosures fell sharply in 2025 and 2026 amid increased federal scrutiny of private-sector DEI, even though federal protections and obligations for veteran hiring remained. Case studies suggest that some firms had housed veteran programs alongside other DEI activities and drew on the same staff and resources.

Corporate foundations direct little of their grantmaking to veteran causes. Veteran-related grants account for less than 1 percent of observed S&P 500 foundation giving, and most active corporate foundations direct no grant dollars to veteran causes.

Protected veteran hiring at S&P 500 contractors remained below national planning benchmarks. S&P contractors’ 2025 new-hire share stood at 2.4 percent, compared with the 5.1 percent national benchmark that took effect that July.

More military-related federal business does not reliably translate into stronger veteran support. Industries with larger military-related federal contracts do not consistently disclose more, give more, or report higher protected veteran employment.

Public data capture veteran hiring far better than they capture retention or advancement.

Recommendations

Issue federal guidance clarifying that veteran hiring and support programs remain lawful and distinct from DEI restrictions. Interviews with corporate veteran program leaders suggest that some companies have treated recent executive-order guidance on DEI as if it also applied to veteran hiring programs; this interpretation has no clear legal basis. The Vietnam Era Veterans’ Readjustment Assistance Act remains federal law, and veteran preferences occupy a distinct legal position from race- or sex-based employment preferences.

Congress and the Department of Labor should update VETS-4212 reporting for large contractors to include category-specific counts of protected veteran employees and new hires, along with 12- and 24-month retention, promotion rates, and management representation.

Publish large-contractor veteran employment outcomes in a centralized database searchable by company, parent firm, industry, contract size, and filing year.

Require a light-touch Form 10-K human-capital disclosure table for publicly traded federal contractors above a contract threshold. The table should report veteran hires, workforce representation, management representation, and year-over-year retention.

Adopt a standardized procurement disclosure for large defense contractors. This report finds little systematic relationship between military contract exposure and observable veteran support. Large defense contractors should report standardized information on veteran hiring, retention, advancement, military-related philanthropy, volunteer activity, and chief executive officer or board oversight.

Develop a standardized voluntary reporting template for veteran-related corporate giving. The public tax data analyzed here capture only grants made through identifiable corporate foundations.

For companies, build veteran employment programs with dedicated staff, senior support, and measurable goals.

items.title: What the Record Shows on Corporate Veteran Support
items.author: Jeffrey B. Wenger
items.summary: Focusing on S&P 500 firms, RAND researchers analyzed public data on what companies say about veteran support, how their foundations give to veteran causes, and the extent to which federal contractors hire protected veterans.
items.body:
George Zuo , Jeffrey B. Wenger

Research Summary Published Sep 9, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Large corporations have the scale and reach to shape veterans’ transitions into civilian careers, and many publicly commit to hiring and supporting veterans. Focusing on Standard and Poor’s 500 (S&P 500) firms, RAND researchers analyzed publicly available data on what companies say about veteran support, how their foundations give to veteran causes, and the extent to which federal contractors hire protected veterans.

Here's what the data shows:

What companies say about veteran support only weakly aligns with how they give and hire. Companies with stronger veteran messaging do not consistently direct more foundation giving to veteran causes or report higher protected veteran hiring rates, and these companies rarely report verifiable retention or advancement outcomes.

Corporate foundations direct little of their grantmaking to veteran causes. Veteran-related grants account for less than 1 percent of observed S&P 500 foundation giving, and most active corporate foundations direct no grant dollars to veteran causes.

Protected veteran hiring at S&P 500 contractor establishments remained below the national planning benchmark for federal contractors. In the 2025 hiring cycle, protected veterans accounted for 2.4 percent of new hires, compared with the 5.1 percent national benchmark.

More military-related federal business does not reliably translate into stronger observable veteran support. Industries with greater military-related contract exposure do not consistently disclose more, give more, or hire more veterans.

The broader diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) retreat may have spilled over to veteran disclosures and programs. High-quality veteran disclosures fell sharply in 2025 and the first half of 2026 amid increased federal scrutiny of private-sector DEI, even though federal protections and obligations for veteran hiring remained. Case studies suggest that some firms had housed veteran programs alongside other DEI activities and drew on the same staff and resources.

Public data capture veteran hiring far better than they capture retention or advancement. Federally required contractor reports provide standardized head counts and new-hire counts for protected veterans at federal contractors, but these reports do not track whether veterans stay or advance. Corporate disclosures almost never voluntarily provide that information.

These findings highlight the limits of the public record and do not provide a complete assessment of any company’s veteran programs. The full report outlines federal policy options for strengthening disclosures to provide a fuller view of veteran hiring, retention, advancement, and investment.

items.title: How States Align Postsecondary and Workforce Strategies
items.author: Gopal Trital
items.summary: The authors analyze all Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act plans across five plan cycles, identifying strategies that policymakers can use to benchmark plans and strengthen coordination between postsecondary education and workforce systems.
items.body:
The authors analyze all Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) plans submitted by U.S. states and territories for Program Years 2016–2027. They identify strategies across five domains: governance, information provision, connecting education to workforce systems, access to learner supports, and employer engagement. The report offers benchmarks for WIOA planners to strengthen cross-agency postsecondary and workforce policy integration.

How States Align Postsecondary and Workforce Strategies

Examples and Trends from WIOA Plans

Elaine W. Leigh , Jeremy Wright-Kim , Laura Rodriguez Lora , Gopal Trital

Research Published Sep 9, 2026

Includes Annex

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

State policymakers want to align postsecondary education and workforce development systems, yet limited research systematically examines how states do so. This report presents a first-ever analysis of Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) plans submitted by U.S. states and territories to the U.S. Department of Labor for Program Years 2016–2027. The authors organize state strategies across five domains: governance, information provision, connecting education to workforce systems, access to learner supports, and employer engagement.

Findings reveal that states generally comply with WIOA plan requirements: Nearly all WIOA plans emphasize career pathways, apprenticeships, and governance structures, and states broadly agree on using employer subsidies to support engagement and provide information to job seekers. More-distinctive strategies include providing incentives for intermediaries to sustain deeper workforce partnerships, attending to adult learner transitions, and offering novel credential options, such as community college baccalaureates.

These findings offer new evidence on peer-state practices for workforce development staff in federal and state agencies who are responsible for WIOA planning and for other state higher education agency staff who must coordinate with workforce agencies. State WIOA planners can benchmark their WIOA plans against these national patterns and find example strategies from other states in a separate annex that support opportunities to strengthen cross-agency planning as federal postsecondary and workforce policy become increasingly integrated.

Key Takeaways

Federal requirements drive consistency in state planning

States almost universally comply with WIOA plan content requirements; nearly all WIOA state plans address career pathways, apprenticeships, and governance structures.

Non-required strategies vary

Although most state plans include mention of employer funds and subsidies to offset the costs of providing training services (97 percent), offering job search tools (94 percent), and discussing access to career counseling (92 percent), only some plans emphasize adult basic education (21 percent) or credit for prior learning (54 percent)—approaches critical for adult learner success.

Seven states—Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, New Jersey, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Texas—demonstrated more-expansive planning approaches

These states emphasized not only federally mandated strategies but also non-required and novel approaches in their WIOA plans. They consistently complied with federal guidelines and appear to be proactive in their attempts to align their postsecondary education and workforce development systems in alternative ways.

Plan type and political context shape some strategy emphasis

States with Combined Plans emphasized interagency collaboration and access to training provider information more than states with Unified Plans. Democrat-led states emphasized information and access to learner supports more consistently, while Republican-led states were more likely to emphasize skills training and financial aid supports.

Recommendations

Treat WIOA planning as a strategic exercise, not just a compliance requirement. States could consider aligning plan development timelines with state strategic planning processes so that workforce priorities inform broader economic development goals.

Strengthen collaborative governance regardless of plan type. Workforce policymakers can use plan submission and modification timelines to establish at least one concrete mechanism to formalize cross-agency coordination.

Reassess credit articulation strategies to adapt to changing learner needs. States should ensure that shifts toward competency-based or credit for prior learning approaches do not inadvertently reduce pathways for traditional-age populations while considering how to scale such efforts.

Move beyond broad career pathways language to specific program designs. Federal guidance should more explicitly help states prioritize two to three priority sectors and provide templates for documenting the specific credentials in the pathway and their labor market value.

Document specific mechanisms for addressing nonacademic barriers. States should use their planning process to create an inventory of support services available to WIOA program participants.

More explicitly align financial aid strategies with workforce development goals. States should address how states’ need-based and short-term or noncredit financial aid programs can support WIOA goals when outlining their plan strategies.

Diversify employer engagement and invest in intermediary capacities. States should use their WIOA planning process to specify who will be responsible to support intermediary capacity-building and how short- and long-term progress will be assessed.

items.title: Justice for All: An anthology
items.author: Lucy Strang
items.summary: This paper draws together the findings of the Justice for All series, reflecting on the contribution of each briefing paper exploring the evidence on the matters under consideration and the key themes that emerge across them.
items.body:
Lucy Strang

Expert Insights Published Sep 9, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Over the past year, the Justice for All series, hosted by the Sheriff of the City of London, has brought together senior leaders from government, business, academia, law enforcement and the justice sector. Framed around Magna Carta and the United Nation's Sustainable Development Goal 16, the series sought to shed light on what a just society requires from us all, and what will it cost us if we do not deliver it.

Each event in the series focused on a specific aspect of the justice system and was accompanied by a research briefing paper exploring the evidence on the matters under consideration. The five papers traced a single argument, across different settings, that the effective delivery of justice makes economic as well as moral sense. This paper draws together the findings of that series, reflecting on the contribution of each briefing and the key themes that emerge across them.

items.title: Iran says it captured US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz
items.author: Idrees Ali and Joe Brock, Reuters
items.summary: Iran said Tuesday it captured a U.S. uncrewed submarine in the Strait of Hormuz. The Pentagon said it had malfunctioned more than a day ago.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

Iran says it captured US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz

An unmanned U.S. submersible that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it captured at the entrance of the Strait of Hormuz, at an undisclosed location in Iran, in this picture obtained on Sept. 8, 2026. (IRGC/West Asia News Agency/handout via Reuters)

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday it had captured a U.S. uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz , offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations.

Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD , a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defense firm Anduril . The 19-foot (5.8-metre) submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.

“We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies,” the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.

In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had “malfunctioned more than a day ago.”

“It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said.

Reuters could not independently verify Iran’s claims and the Pentagon did not address them in its statement.

Anduril did not respond to a request for comment.

The U.S. military is investing heavily in unmanned naval systems, including underwater and surface vessels, as it seeks cheaper ways to monitor vast areas of ocean, gather intelligence and track adversary ships and submarines without putting sailors at risk.

According to Anduril’s website, Dive-LD can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and is designed to dive to depths of as much as 6,000 metres (19,700 feet). Dive-LD units cost about $2.5 million each, U.S. military news site DefenseScoop reported in 2024.

items.title: US Strikes 5 Iranian Oil Tankers as More Fighter Jets Ordered to Middle East
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: In a dramatic flare-up in the hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan. The post US Strikes 5 Iranian Oil Tankers as More Fighter Jets Ordered to Middle East appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

In a dramatic flare-up in the fighting between the U.S. and Iran, American forces struck and destroyed five Iranian oil tankers Sept. 8, U.S. Central Command said. Iran retaliated by lobbing ballistic missiles toward a major U.S. base in Jordan.

U.S. officials said CENTCOM took the action because Iran had fired ballistic missiles against a U.S. Navy warship twice in the past two days. The ship, which the U.S. military did not identify, was not hit, and no service members were harmed, CENTCOM said.

Nevertheless, the U.S. hit back with a major attack on Iranian shipping.

“CENTCOM destroyed the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman as well as M/T Derya near Kharg Island,” the command said in a statement, referring to ships controlled by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. CENTCOM released a video of the attacks, which shows several ships engulfed in flames.

The Iranian ships were attacked by U.S. Air Force and Navy fighters and drones.

The U.S. military said the crews were directed to abandon ship before the vessels were “rendered inoperable.”

“Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM added. The command also delivered a harsh warning to Tehran: “Iran has no means by which to defend these vessels.”

Repeated, escalating tit-for-tat strikes in recent days have raised the risk that the two sides might resume the all-out fighting that characterized the first weeks of the war, which is now in its seventh month.

The Trump administration has adopted a policy of striking Iranian tankers to deter Iran from firing missiles at the aircraft carriers in the region and other Navy ships . On Sept. 5, Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads U.S. Central Command, warned the U.S. would “impose an even higher economic cost” on Iran by striking a “limited and exposed oil fleet” if Tehran did not cease its attacks on U.S. forces.

But that warning went unheeded.

In response to the latest U.S. attack, the Iranian military vowed to carry out fresh strikes of its own, specifically against long-standing American allies like Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain. Iranian officials also warned that it would target commercial oil tankers near ports in these countries. Iranian officials said such attacks would be justified because those ports had been used by the U.S.

Jordan was hardest hit as Iran fired dozens of ballistic missiles at the country. Iran said it was targeting Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a key hub for U.S. airpower. Dramatic videos from Jordan showed ballistic missiles and interceptors filling the night sky. Without providing evidence, the IRGC claimed it damaged American fighter aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti, known as MSAB. No American personnel were killed in the intense barrage aimed at the base, according to initial accounts from U.S. officials.

The Trump administration has hoped that stepped-up economic sanctions and its ongoing blockade would force Iranians to stop interfering with traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and to make other concessions. But Tehran has shown no sign of backing down.

The U.S. is deploying fresh warplanes to the Middle East amid the fighting. F-35 Lightning II stealth fighters from the 115th Fighter Wing of the Wisconsin Air National Guard are deploying to the region and are set to arrive in the Middle East in the coming days, people familiar with the matter said.

The Wisconsin Air Guardsmen are replacing another F-35 unit, the 158th Fighter Wing of the Vermont Air National Guard. Vermont’s “Green Mountain Boys” wrapped up a roughly nine-month deployment to South America and the Middle East, where it supported the capture of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro before heading to the Middle East to fight Iran. Airmen from the unit returned home Sept. 6 and were greeted by Chief of the National Guard Bureau Air Force Gen. Steven Nordhaus.

The fresh F-35s are not the only new fighter unit reinforcing America’s posture in the Middle East. F-16s from the Ohio Air National Guard’s 180th Fighter Wing deployed to the Middle East late last week, taking the place of F-16s from the 555th Fighter Squadron of the 31st Fighter Wing, which returned home to Aviano Air Base, Italy. Nicknamed the “Triple Nickel,” the 555th Fighter Squadron had been deployed to the Middle East since last November, a long deployment compared to the Air Force’s typical six-month rotations.

The Air Force has dozens of F-16, F-35, and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and A-10 Thunderbolt II attack planes deployed to the Middle East, along with support aircraft and scores of tankers. More rotations are expected in the coming weeks.

The U.S. Navy also has two aircraft carriers and their embarked carrier air wings supporting operations in the Middle East: the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, along with around 20 surface vessels.

Like the Air Force, the Navy has also had extended deployments in the Middle East to carry out operations against Iran. The USS Abraham Lincoln is headed home after a nine-month deployment. Before that, the USS Gerald R. Ford was deployed for 11 months and, like Vermont’s Air Force unit, supported operations against both Venezuela and Iran.

As the U.S. and Iran exchanged blows, the U.S. Treasury Department announced it was imposing new sanctions on companies that support Mahan Air, an airline that U.S. officials say is connected to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Fresh fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia added to the tension in the region. The Iran-backed Houthis fired missiles and drones at energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Sept. 8.

items.title: Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints
items.author: Tobias Naegele
items.summary: The Department of the Air Force's new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's directives, redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints. The post Air Force EO Overhaul Lets Commanders Dismiss Some Complaints appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Department of the Air Force’s new equal opportunity and harassment policy, rolled out to comply with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s directives , redefines key terms and empowers commanders to dismiss complaints they deem not actionable. The new rules also bar investigations based on anonymous complaints.

Unveiled 11 months after Hegseth directed changes to the Pentagon’s Equal Opportunity and Military Equal Opportunity programs, the new rules are dated July 28, but weren’t announced until late August. Hegseth called for the overhaul nearly a year ago, saying the programs had been “ weaponized ” by poor performers against leaders and commanders.

“No more frivolous complaints, no more anonymous complaints, no more repeat complaints, no more smearing reputations, no more endless waiting, no more legal limbo, no more side-tracking careers, no more walking on eggshells,” Hegseth said last Sept. 30 at an all-call with hundreds of generals and admirals .

The Department of the Air Force policy follows on similar updates from the Army and Navy , also announced in August.

New Definitions

Each military department’s policy includes the same new definitions of three key terms: “bullying,” “hazing,” and “harassment.”

The new definition of harassment represents the biggest change, said retired Lt. Col. Colby Volkey, a former Marine Corps Judge Advocate General. The new definition explicitly exempts standard training programs, stating “official military or governmental activities conducted in a professional manner, such as basic military training, professional military education, physical training programs, disciplinary or corrective actions, or combat readiness exercises, do not constitute harassment.”

It also states that “behavior that is rude, ignorant, abrasive, or unkind, is not necessarily indicative of harassment, but may constitute harassment depending on the totality of the circumstances.”

The revisions appear to be “an attempt to limit the types of activities that are considered harassment, Volkey said in an email.

The new definition of hazing no longer includes the phrase “any form or initiations or congratulatory acts that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same,” language that was included in the past in an effort to stop the practice of pounding on newly earned rank or other insignia, such as aviators’ wings.

Equal Opportunity Definition Changes

Bullying

Bullying: As described in DoDI 1020.03, while not a form of prohibited harassment under equal opportunity (EO) law but is a prohibited form of conduct, bullying is a form of harassment that includes acts of aggression by service members or DoD civilian employees, with a nexus to military service, with the intent of harming a service member either physically or psychologically, without a proper military or other governmental purpose. Bullying may involve the singling out of an individual from his or her coworkers, or unit, for ridicule because he or she is considered different or weak. It often involves an imbalance of power between the aggressor and the victim. Bullying can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.

Bullying is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:

Physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.

Intimidating, teasing, or taunting another person.

Oral or written berating of another person with the purpose of belittling or humiliating.

Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning, or dangerous acts.

Playing abusive or malicious tricks.

Branding, handcuffing, duct taping, tattooing, shaving, greasing, or painting another person.

Subjecting another person to excessive or abusive use of water.

Forcing another person to consume food, alcohol, drugs, or any other substance.

Degrading or damaging another’s property or reputation.

Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of bullying.

Bullying does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., command-authorized physical training). Service members may be responsible for an act of bullying even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Bullying is prohibited in all circumstances and environments, including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.

Bullying (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves repetitive, intentional hurtful conduct by an individual or a group, which intimidates, humiliates, torments, isolates, degrades, exploits, controls, or creates a risk of mental, physical, or emotional distress or harm.

Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical pain or injury.

Berating or belittling a Service member’s duty performance, professional abilities, or personal attributes.

Threatening, teasing, or taunting a Service member.

Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverable.

Excluding a Service member from work-related opportunities, information, or social activities.

Posting malicious gossip, rumors, and lies on social media, sharing humiliating photos, or sending vicious text messages

Harassment

Harassment (Military): As described in DoDI 1020.03, conduct that is unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person, whether verbal or nonverbal, written, electronic, or physical, that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment. Harassment may include offensive jokes, epithets, ridicule or mockery, insults or put-downs, displays of offensive objects or imagery, stereotyping, intimidating acts, veiled threats of violence, threatening or provoking remarks, racial or other slurs, derogatory remarks about a person’s accent, or displays of racially offensive symbols.

Types of harassment include, but are not limited to, discriminatory harassment, sexual harassment, hazing, bullying, stalking, revenge porn, and other sexual misconduct. Stalking, Revenge Porn, Other Sexual Misconduct. Formal complaints involving conduct that may be punishable under Articles 130 (stalking); 117a (wrongful broadcast or distribution of intimate visual images); and 120c (other sexual misconduct) of the UCMJ will be referred to the appropriate military criminal investigative organization or other law enforcement organization with criminal investigators who are specially trained to conduct such investigations. Harassment can be oral, written, or physical. Harassment can occur in person, through electronic communications, including social media, and other forms of communication. Activities or actions undertaken for a proper military or governmental purpose, such as combat survival training, making work assignments, or conducting performance counseling are generally not considered harassment. For the purpose of this publication, the DAF MEO program is limited to processing complaints alleging bullying and hazing as “other forms of harassment.”

Harassment (Military): Conduct by a Service member or civilian employee, without a legitimate military or governmental purpose, that would be unwelcome or offensive to a reasonable person in the military environment, whether delivered verbally or nonverbally, including by written or electronic means, or in-person, that creates an intimidating, humiliating, or abusive environment.

Hazing

Hazing—As described in DoDI 1020.03, hazing is a form of harassment that includes conduct through which service members or DoD employees, without a proper military or other governmental purpose, but with a nexus to military service, physically or psychologically injure or create a risk of physical or psychological injury to service members for the purpose of: initiation into, admission into, affiliation with, change in status or position within, or continued membership in any military or DoD civilian organization. Hazing can be conducted through the use of electronic devices or communications, and by other means including social media, as well as in person.

Hazing is evaluated by a reasonable person standard and includes, but is not limited to, the following when performed without a proper military or other governmental purpose:

Any form of initiation or congratulatory act that involves physically striking another person in any manner or threatening to do the same.

Pressing any object into another person’s skin, regardless of whether it pierces the skin, such as “pinning” or “tacking on” of rank insignia, aviator wings, jump wings, diver insignia, badges, medals, or any other object.

Encouraging another person to engage in illegal, harmful, demeaning or dangerous acts.

Soliciting, coercing, or knowingly permitting another person to solicit or coerce acts of hazing.

Hazing does not include properly directed command or organizational activities that serve a proper military or other governmental purpose, or the requisite training activities required to prepare for such activities (e.g., administrative corrective measures, extra military instruction, or command-authorized physical training). Service members or DoD civilian employees may be responsible for an act of hazing, even if there was actual or implied consent from the victim, and regardless of the grade or rank, status, or service of the victim. Hazing is prohibited in all circumstances and environments including off-duty or “unofficial” unit functions and settings.

Hazing (Military): A form of harassment, as described below, that involves intentional or reckless conduct by an individual or group, which humiliates, degrades, or creates mental, physical, or psychological injury or harm, or reasonably perceived as such, directly related to the affected Service member’s affiliation, entry, advancement, reinstatement, change in status or position, or continued standing within a military unit, command, or DoW or military affiliated organizations regardless of whether the affected Service member consented to the activity.

Inflicting or threatening to inflict physical violence, including striking, restraining, branding, causing body modifications, tattooing, shaving, greasing, duct taping, or engaging in any form of unwanted physical contact that causes pain or injury.

Subjecting a Service member to abusive physical discomfort or fatigue.

Destroying or confiscating a Service member’s personal property or work equipment or deliverables.

Requiring financial contributions.

Dismissing Complaints

The new policy instructs installation commanders to dismiss formal equal opportunity complaints in certain circumstances, such as if:

The complaint “does not contain sufficient or actionable information to investigate.”

“A complainant does not respond to request for information.”

“A complainant files duplicative or related complaints”

If a commander or supervisor to the service member making the complaint determines “through an adverse action or UCMJ action” that the complaint was a false official statement

Under the new policy, equal opportunity directors have five days to review a formal complaint before forwarding it to an installation commander, who in turn has 30 days to consult with the “servicing legal officer’ and determine if the complaint should be dismissed. The commander then has seven days to inform the complainant, who in turn has five days to appeal.

Giving commanders the power to dismiss complaints is a radical change, said David Sheldon, a former Navy JAG who now represents military clients from every service branch as a civilian attorney. The policy leaves it up to commanders to make a legal determination over whether the complaint is “sufficient or actionable.” Indeed, Congress only recently determined that commanders were not well suited to prosecute certain serious crimes, including murder, sexual assault, and domestic violence.

“It’s kind of a step in the wrong direction in my thinking, for the very reason that you have a conflict of interest,” Sheldon said. Commanders have a built-in incentive not to be seen as having EO problems within their commands, he said.

Dismissing or resolving a case removes the holds that have sometimes delayed promotions, held key jobs opened, or resulted in foreshortened careers. Once closed, the policy states, “all favorable administrative personnel actions (e.g., awards, promotion, retirements) for an alleged offender of an [Military Equal Opportunity] complaint will be resumed or completed.”

Similarly, an individual being under investigation for an EO complaint is no longer sufficient grounds to withhold awards, promotions, retirement and other favorable actions. In the past, EO complaints have resulted in holds that could remain in place for months.

Anonymous Complaints vs. Confidential Reports

The new policy eliminates military equal opportunity complaints based on anonymous allegations, with some exceptions. Instead of filing anonymously, service members may submit “confidential reports,” revealing their identities only to equal opportunity directors and staff. But confidential reports do not constitute either informal or formal complaints, and therefore cannot trigger an investigation. Rather, they are merely a means for service members “to disclose allegations, receive information regarding available resources and reporting options, and obtain referrals to appropriate support services,” the policy states.

Commanders may choose to “look into the matter and take appropriate action in response to a referred anonymous report of prohibited discrimination or discriminatory harassment,” and a service member can choose, within time limits, to upgrade a confidential report into a complaint.

Allegations regarding sexual harassment and those concerning bullying or hazing are not covered by that limitation, however. Anonymous allegations regarding sexual harassment must be referred to the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response office. Allegations of bullying and harassment can be anonymous, but must include “sufficient information,” such as the offender’s name and rank, date of the incident, and units involved.

Shorter Timeline

The timeline for service members to file complaints is now shorter, just 60 days versus 90 days previously. But there are exceptions:

Multiple incidents: In cases involving an alleged series of incidents or pattern of behavior, only one instance needs to have taken place within the past 60 days.

Deployments: Service members who are deployed when an incident occurs and who lack resources at their deployed locations have 60 days to file once they return.

Delays: Those who waited too long can submit a memo to their installation commander explaining the circumstances and seek an extension.

Sexual harassment: By law, these complaints are exempt from the 60-day requirement.

A service member who makes a confidential complaint and then wants to formalize it, must do so within 60 days of the incident—not the report.

Sheldon suggested this makes it harder for complainants. Whether it is 45, 60, or 90 days, he said, “obviously “I would like a longer window just to give the aggrieved party an opportunity to be heard.”

Mediation

The new policy opens the door for “facilitation,” a form of mediation in which a neutral third party meets with the accused and the complainant to try to resolve the conflict. Facilitation is “a method for resolving problematic situations before they rise to the level of misconduct,” the policy states.

The confidential process can be offered for both informal and formal complaints, so long as both parties agree; commanders are instructed to consult with their legal offices before determining if it is a suitable solution for a given complaint. Commanders may also forgo facilitation if they determine it would “negatively impact good order and discipline.”

items.title: Ukraine contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defense chief says
items.author: Reuters
items.summary: Ukraine is contracting a supply of around 1,000 missiles for U.S.-designed Patriot air-defence systems.
items.body:
Europe

Ukraine contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defense chief says

The 37th Air Defense Missile Squadron's Patriot missile systems, at the 3rd Warsaw Air Defense Missile Brigade's base in Sochaczew, Poland, on Dec. 18, 2025. (Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Jacek Marczewski via Reuters)

Ukraine is contracting a supply of around 1,000 missiles for U.S.-designed Patriot air-defence systems with the help of allies and through a European Union loan, Kyiv’s defense minister said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Yevhenii Khmara also said that the majority of the missiles would only be shipped in the coming years, and called for more urgent aid.

In comments posted later by the Defence Ministry, Khmara said Ukraine was asking its Western partners to provide more air defense missiles from their stocks in exchange for improvements in missile performance under contracts signed with Kyiv.

He said Ukraine was being hindered by a shortfall of $27 billion in financing for drone supplies.

RELATED

Brussels is weighing a rare waiver that would let Kyiv tap its €90 billion loan for U.S.-made interceptors for the first time.

Khmara said Russia was making no strategic gains along the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line, but Moscow was making up for its battlefield failures with “terror against Ukrainians.”

items.title: First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: After months of delays, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore. The post First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Editor’s Note: This article has been updated to include a comment from Boeing.

After months of delays from a factory strike, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore.

“This is an important next step toward bringing the F-15EX home to Kadena,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said in a release. “Our team is ready to welcome the F-15EX, and this is another milestone that brings us closer to putting this capability in the hands of the Airmen who will fly, maintain and employ it from Japan.”

The F-15EX is the first Eagle II jet to feature the 18th Wing’s historic, distinctive “ZZ” tail flash and will actually arrive at Kadena sometime in fiscal 2027, which begins Oct. 1.

Spokespeople for Headquartes Air Force, the 18th Wing, and the Air National Guard did not immediately respond to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine on Sept. 8.

Boeing spokesman Josh Roth told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the F-15EX-22 “was delivered with the baseline mission computing, communications, and sensor capabilities that provide the foundation for manned-unmanned teaming and future Collaborative Combat Aircraft integration.” He deferred additional questions to the Air Force.

This new jet is the first of 36 F-15EXs to be stationed at Kadena. The fighter, often described as halfway between fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft, will help usher in a new era in U.S. airpower within the first island chain surrounding China

The transition to the EX has been a long time coming for Kadena—the Air Force started retiring the base’s legacy F-15C/Ds in 2022 and confirmed plans to replace them with the F-15EX in 2024. The first jet was supposed to arrive in spring 2026, but a lengthy strike at the Boeing plant in St. Louis late last year slowed production until this Aug. 28 delivery.

The new F-15EX’s stopover in Oregon isn’t surprising—the Oregon Air National Guard was the first Air Force location with combat-coded F-15EXs at its Portland ANG Base. The base will conduct the final systems integration, add software updates, and other technical preparations before the aircraft can go to Okinawa.

In the interim, the Air Force has rotated F-16, F-15, F-22, and F-35 squadrons through Kadena to keep the tactical fighter presence steady at a key strategic base fewer than 400 miles from Taiwan.

Those rotational forces haven’t always matched the capabilities the F-15EX will bring. Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on the extended tour of aging F-16Cs out of the Colorado Air National Guard’s 120th Fighter Squadron, which ran from January through June. They brought a dozen fighters.

Both the squadron commander and the head of its parent wing, the 140th Wing, said in a call with the media on Sept. 3 that while the platform could keep up with fifth-gen fighters in the region, the pilots and maintenance crews were pushing the limits of the more than 30-year-old airframe

The permanent stationing of the F-15EX will “enhance Kadena’s ability to generate ready combat airpower while providing opportunities to train and integrate alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other allies and partners,” according to the release.

The 18th Wing trains alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15s at Naha Air Base in bilateral exercises and other training, according to the release.

Pacific Air Forces has been slowly phasing out its oldest fighters and introducing more modern jets in recent years. In addition to Kadena’s F-15s, the Air Force has also recently withdrawn the A-10s at Osan Air Base, South Korea.

The 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa Air Base, Japan, meanwhile, is slated to get 48 fifth-gen F-35 Lightning IIs, but only a trickle had arrived as of April. The wing transferred its F-16s to Osan last year .

The Air Force publicly confirmed delays in getting the F-15EX to Kadena in February .

The Eagle II is the first of its kind to include digital fly-by-wire flight controls, a large-area display glass cockpit with a touchscreen interface, an APG-82 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar, a Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, and an Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System.

The jet flies faster and farther, carries a heavier payload than its F-15 predecessors, and has two additional weapons stations.

items.title: Space Force Expects to Spend $17B More on Launch as Demand Soars
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force expects the scope of its main launch program to grow by 91 missions and nearly $17 billion by fiscal 2032 as demand for national security space capabilities soars. The post Space Force Expects to Spend $17B More on Launch as Demand Soars appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force expects the scope of its main launch program to grow by 91 missions and nearly $17 billion by fiscal 2032 as demand for national security space capabilities soars.

Those increases are revealed in the latest version of the National Security Space Launch program’s selected acquisition report , drafted in April and published in September. The update brings NSSL’s total expected procurement to $76 billion for 337 launches between fiscal 2004 and 2032.

At the same time, the average cost per launch is dropping significantly, from around $422 million in 2022 to $192 million in the most recent report. That average combines a range of vehicle and payload configurations, which means some missions are much cheaper and others more expensive.

The surge in demand comes as the Space Force is planning to field large numbers of satellites in the coming years to support missions like satellite communications, space domain awareness, missile warning, and moving target indication. NSSL also supports the National Reconnaissance Office and other classified customers who are fielding proliferated constellations of their own.

The Space Force in recent months has acknowledged that its NSSL contracts will need to grow to accommodate that demand. The program has two competitive tracks, or lanes: Lane 1 is reserved for commercial-like missions with higher risk tolerance, whereas Lane 2 serves more demanding customers flying high-value payloads with less margin for error.

In July, the service announced it would triple the size of its Lane 1 contract ceiling from $5.6 billion to $17 billion, increasing the number of missions from early estimates of between 30 and 60 to approximately 170 launches over a five-year period. Likewise, “emergent requirements” are driving the service to increase the number of Lane 2 by 25—from 54 to 79.

The Space Force hasn’t said which programs these launches will support, but it has announced several contracts in recent months to buy satellites that will need rides to space over the next few years. In late May, it awarded SpaceX a $2.3 billion contract to build out its Space Data Network constellation and a $4.2 billion contract for its Space-Based AMTI program. The service also plans to launch new fleets of small surveillance and reconnaissance satellites under an effort called Andromeda, with the initial spacecraft slated to launch in 2029. The Space Force hasn’t said how many spacecraft those constellations will include, but it has set a contract ceiling of approximately $6 billion.

The growing manifest is also likely to support Golden Dome, a sprawling, layered, missile defense architecture. The Space Force is supporting that program in a few ways, including by developing space-based interceptors that can engage a missile during the boost and midcourse phases of flight. Initial prototypes of those spacecraft are expected to be integrated into the Golden Dome architecture by 2028.

The Space Development Agency is also fielding a missile defense and tracking constellation and recently announced it would add 36 more satellites to that architecture to support Golden Dome. Those satellites are also scheduled to be ready for launch by 2028.

Whether these satellites launch on time hinges, in part, on the availability of certified, ready rockets. To qualify to fly Lane 1 missions, companies need to have successfully launched their vehicle at least once. Lane 2 missions, however, require certification from the Space Force, a lengthy process that requires multiple launches. To date, only SpaceX and ULA are eligible to launch satellites for both lanes, though ULA’s Vulcan rocket is currently grounded due to an anomaly on a February NSSL launch.

Blue Origin’s New Glenn is eligible for Lane 1 flights and is on the certification path for Lane 2, but it, too, is grounded after a rocket exploded on the pad in May . Four other companies—including Rocket Lab, Stoke Space, Impulse Space, and Relativity Space—are on deck to compete for missions as soon as their developmental rockets complete at least one launch.

That leaves SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy as the only rockets available to support NSSL missions at the moment. The Space Force is weighing near-term options to mitigate schedule delays caused by Vulcan’s grounding—including swapping some missions to SpaceX rockets—but several programs have already seen delays. For example, the launch of the first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites, slated for March, has been pushed to no sooner than October.

Brig. Gen. Eric Zarybnisky, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space access, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July that he is “worried about timelines,” particularly for the more urgent Lane 2 missions.

“Those are vastly important national security assets that we need to get to orbit,” he said.

items.title: Poland’s in-development fighting vehicle carries newfound defense-export drive
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Polish officials hope a new infantry fighting vehicle design will propel the country's weapons-export business.
items.body:
Europe

Poland’s in-development fighting vehicle carries newfound defense-export drive

Visitors look at armored vehicles on display at the MSPO defense show in Kielce, Poland, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Jaroslaw Adamowski/staff)

KIELCE, Poland — As Poland’s defense spending has reached record levels , the country aims to increasingly shift from the role of a buyer of foreign military gear to its exporter, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and National Defence Minister, said on the opening day of this year’s MSPO show here.

The technology demonstrator for a new heavy tracked infantry fighting vehicle, developed by Poland’s industry and presented during the event, reflects this ambition.

“Poland is becoming a country that not only buys military gear from the world, but is also its major producer,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said at the show’s opening ceremony on Sept. 8.

The deputy prime minister said the Polish defense industry can benefit from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme. Under the instrument, Poland has been allocated up to €43.7 billion ($50.8 billion) worth of low-interest loans for military acquisitions.

“We have reached a level of fifty-fifty [between domestic military gear purchases and imports]. This would not happen without the SAFE mechanism,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

The Polish sector is dominated by state-owned defense group PGZ but also features a group of emerging private companies.

Kosiniak-Kamysz named PGZ’s new heavy tracked infantry fighting vehicle (IFV), whose technology demonstrator was officially presented during this year’s MSPO event, as one of the examples of the Polish industry’s potential flagship export products.

“This is a modern platform, with a weight of between 40 and 43 tons, which maximizes troop protection,” a PGZ representative told Defense News. “We plan to present the vehicle’s prototype next year, and it could enter serial production in 2029.”

The heavy IFV is to be added to PGZ’s offer alongside the group’s light tracked IFV, the Borsuk (Badger) , that is already in production. To date, the Polish Ministry of National Defence has ordered 257 Borsuks from the group, with deliveries of up to 1,400 units of the platform in different variants envisioned ina 2023 framework agreement.

Military officials expect around 700 heavy IFVs could be procured for the Polish Army.

While Poland’s pro-European Union government is advancing efforts to ramp up domestic weapons, equipment and ammunition production, while also intensify cooperation with European partners, the country remains a major buyer of gear from the United States.

Over the past years, Poland has placed orders for Abrams tanks , F-35 fighter jets , AH-64E Apache helicopters , Patriot missiles and M142 HIMARS rocket launchers , among other equipment.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: Hanwha plans to build armored vehicle carrying a counter-drone laser
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Hanwha representatives said the vehicle is fitted with a more powerful version of the stationary Cheongwang laser that protects the presidential compound.
items.body:
Europe

Hanwha plans to build armored vehicle carrying a counter-drone laser

South Korea's Hanwha brought models of the company's air-defense products to the MSPO defense trade show in Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. (Hanwha)

KIELCE, Poland — As Poland and numerous other NATO eastern flank countries are looking for inexpensive ways to bolster their counter-drone capabilities, South Korea’s Hanwha is pitching a new product to militaries across the region: a 50 kW laser mounted on an armored vehicle.

Speaking on Sept. 8, the first day of the annual MSPO defense industry show in Kielce, Poland, company representatives said the vehicle is fitted with a more powerful version of the stationary Cheongwang laser that South Korea’s military has used since 2024.

Cheongwang has been deployed at strategically important sites, including near the Blue House, the office and residence of the nation’s president.

“We are currently in talks with a number of countries over potential exports of the Cheongwang laser, including potential clients from Europe, Asia and the Middle East,” Hyungun Park, the manager of the laser system business team at Hanwha Systems, told Defense News.

One of the biggest advantages of the Cheongwang results from the fact that each laser shot costs around 2,000 Korean won ($1.5) which makes the weapon a highly cost-efficient way to counter drones, Park said.

To cater to the needs of militaries seeking a mobile laser solution capable of tracking fast-moving targets, the company has combined its laser technology with a wheeled platform, using the Tigon eight-wheel-drive armored personnel carrier.

“Our new product is the 50 kW Laser Armored Vehicle. We have developed a prototype, and we plan to launch serial production of this vehicle by the end of 2027,” according to the executive.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: US Air Force seeks air-defense guns to protect overseas bases
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: The U.S. Air Force plans to acquire anti-aircraft guns to protect its overseas bases following Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the Middle East.
items.body:
Mideast Africa

US Air Force seeks air-defense guns to protect overseas bases

Smoke rises after Iran launched a missile attack targeting the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet in Manama, Bahrain, on Feb. 28, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

In the wake of Iranian attacks that devastated U.S. bases in the Middle East , the U.S. Air Force wants portable air-defense guns that can destroy drones and cruise missiles.

The Ground-Based, Medium-Caliber Gun Weapon System project is aiming for a weapon “that fires affordable munitions, enables defense against air and missile threats with an initial focus on subsonic cruise missiles (CM) and Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) to provide persistent defense in support of United States Air Force assets,” according to the Air Force’s Request for Information published Thursday. The deadline is Oct. 9.

Iran has unleashed retaliatory strikes at U.S. military installations and civilian infrastructure across the Middle East amid bombardment by U.S. and Israeli forces.

U.S. troops were killed when an Iranian one-way attack drone evaded U.S. air defenses and struck a makeshift operations center at a civilian port in Kuwait. More troops were killed in attacks on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia.

The Iranian strikes have also damaged U.S. aircraft , including five KC-135s on the ground at Prince Sultan Air Base.

The Air Force’s RFI doesn’t request a specific caliber for the new weapons system, but “ medium-caliber ” suggests a weapon in the 20mm to 50mm range. In August, the U.S. Army published a Sources Sought notice for a 50mm anti-drone cannon and ammunition. The Army plans to conduct a live-fire test using Northrop Grumman’s XM913 Bushmaster 50mm chain gun, with companies supplying 50mm ammunition.

The Air Force’s weapon will have 15 baseline parameters, including its probability of kill, or PK, against subsonic cruise missiles, as well as Group 1 to Group 5 UAVs, meaning small drones all the way up to very large unmanned aircraft flying above 18,000 feet.

Contractors “must carefully select the organic sensor capability and phenomenology—integrating the right mix of radar, electro-optical, infrared, or radio-frequency sensors—to ensure reliable target acquisition and tracking across varying weather conditions, environments, and countermeasure scenarios,” the Air Force emphasized.

Weapons will also be assessed for range and elevation, magazine capacity, number of crew needed and integration with other sensors and command networks. They must also be capable of stopping saturation attacks by drones and missiles.

The Air Force is also looking for a portable air defense weapon with “a lightweight, modular, and transportable footprint that can be swiftly projected into austere theater environments to meet emergent threats.”

Based on the RFI, the Air Force appears cognizant of modern air defense’s biggest challenge : air defense systems that are either much more expensive than the drones and missiles they are trying to stop, or systems that run out of ammunition before an attacker does.

The new weapon “must optimize munition performance versus munition cost and gun capability, ensuring that the interceptor’s velocity, maneuverability, and terminal effects are maximized without driving the cost-per-engagement to unsustainable levels or exceeding the physical constraints of the host platform,” the RFI said.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: New space strategy will bolster UK defences against threats from space
items.summary: New UK space strategy to bring government's investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back everyday technologies
items.body:
New national space strategy brings together UK’s plans for growth, defence, and national security to help reindustrialise the UK

Government will design a resilient, integrated national satellite communications system to boost our security and defence

Strategy also brings everyday benefits to Brits from better connectivity on trains to stronger phone signals

Safeguarding our national security and defence capabilities are the key pillars of a new strategy launched today (Tuesday 8 September) which puts the UK’s space sector to work in reindustrialising the country over the coming years.

Backed by a record £7.8 billion until 2030, the UK Space Strategy brings government’s space investment and activity under one plan to drive growth, strengthen security and back the technologies that underpin modern life.

It also recognises space as an increasingly important domain for keeping our country safe. Work to strengthen Space Domain Awareness – the study and monitoring of objects like satellites, rockets and debris orbiting our planet – is being backed by projects including £149 million for the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Vigil mission and £85 million for the National Space Operations Centre. UK funding will see British tech offer earlier warnings of potential satellite collisions, hostile activity and solar storms, helping protect the power, communications and navigation services people rely on every day.

Meanwhile £880 million will help beef up the UK’s space control and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities, funding technologies that can track military activity on the ground and potential attacks on satellites, meaning we can act quickly and decisively to protect our way of life on Earth and our assets in space.

A further £2.8 billion meanwhile will go towards strengthening connectivity, including the Connectivity in Low Earth Orbit and SKYNET defence communications programmes, which play a pivotal role in keeping our Armed Forces connected wherever they are in the world.

These benefits will also be felt in everyday life, helping bring faster, more reliable connectivity to rural communities and reducing mobile signal dropouts on trains by using advanced satellite communications.

Together, these investments will help grow a UK space sector worth £18.6 billion and supporting over 55,000 skilled jobs – cementing Britain’s place as a global space leader from satellite services that underpin the economy to landmark missions such as the UK-built Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover.

Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said:

“As space becomes a new frontier of economic and military competition, this plan will help keep Britain secure by strengthening our ability to launch satellites, detect threats and protect the services people rely on every day.

“At the same time, this plan will enable our excellent UK industry to seize the boundless opportunities of this new age in space, creating skilled jobs, driving growth and improving connectivity for all of us.”

Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said:

“This space strategy recognises that our national security depends on our freedom of action in space and, if necessary, the ability to protect UK and allied space assets. As threats in orbit grow more sophisticated, so must our ability to detect and respond to them, ensuring we protect the interests of the UK and allies while fuelling economic growth along the way.

“Backed by the Defence Investment Plan, we’re investing more than £3 billion to ensure our defence capabilities in space keep pace with the threats we face, supporting reindustrialisation and creating opportunities here in the UK.”

The Strategy also offers an opportunity to deliver the jobs and companies of the future, with £40 million to support pioneering in-orbit servicing, assembly and manufacturing technologies (ISAM). These will help repair and maintain satellites damaged by space debris, solar storms or hostile interference, while helping clear dangerous objects from orbit – all while continuing to operate in space.

That support will help bring new products online that are directly developed in the unique environment of space, from new semiconductors that underpin our power grid to pharmaceuticals and drug delivery tools that could transform outcomes for patients.

Additional support for the UK’s wide-ranging space sector includes:

£148 million for European rocket programmes and £30 million for SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland – helping Britain and our partners to launch satellites without relying on countries further afield while creating new jobs.

£163 million in space science and exploration missions, including the delivery of the Rosalind Franklin Mars Rover built in Stevenage. These missions power world-leading research while boosting this government’s mission to reindustrialise the UK with high-skilled jobs and new tech in areas like AI and autonomous systems.

£57 million from the Department for Transport to improve rail connectivity, £190 million from UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) for astronomy and space science research, and £9 million from the Met Office to strengthen space weather forecasting.

For the first time, government will take a single approach to buying and developing space technology, starting with satellite communications, helping British firms win more work, strengthening UK supply chains, supporting skilled jobs and delivering capabilities faster and better value for taxpayers.

The new Strategy formally replaces the previous National Space Strategy, published in 2021, and will play a key role in the delivery of the Modern Industrial Strategy to deliver reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.

Alongside the Strategy, we’re reforming space regulations to reduce costs, reward responsible operators and make it easier for UK firms to invest in cutting-edge missions from satellite servicing to lunar exploration.

Supportive comments:

Doug Liddle, Chair of the trade association UKspace, said:

“UKspace welcomes the publication of the government’s new UK Space Strategy. It sets out a constructive path towards a refreshed approach to space in the UK, which we hope will result in a stronger emphasis on open, inclusive cross-sector dialogue. The new, focussed strategy offers a valuable opportunity to create a more streamlined framework, strengthen collaboration and deliver greater impact across the UK space sector.”

Kevin Craven, CEO of the ADS Group, said:

“We welcome the publication of the new space strategy, and the sustained effort to bring a cross-government perspective to space capability delivery. It is important that government maintains an open, transparent and ambitious partnership with industry to realise its national security and growth goals. “Certainty allows the sector to operate at pace and for its industrial base to make long-term strategic and commercial commitments. It is also a vital signal of intent to our international partners for trade and collaboration. ADS looks forward to supporting government on the crucial next steps for implementation.”

Professor Anna Hogg and Professor Mark Sims, Space Academic Network (SPAN) Co-Chairs said:

“SPAN welcomes the new cross-Government space strategy and its integrated delivery plan. Space technologies and services are integral to modern life, from secure communications to monitoring and responding to environmental change. We look forward to seeing the detail of the strategy and delivery plan, which will be critical in enabling academia and industry to plan, invest and work together to deliver the UK’s ambitions for space. Sustained investment across academia and industry is crucial to creating the cutting-edge technologies, capabilities, talent and growth of the future.”

Joanne Wheeler MBE, Managing Partner at Alden and Director of the Earth & Space Sustainability Initiative, said:

“In addition to enhancing UK security and defence, the UK Space Strategy brings together world-leading innovative regulation and insurance opportunities to enable and drive growth and investment, whilst encouraging responsible and sustainable operations.”

Simon Brown, Met Office Managing Director, said:

“Space based observations are critical for delivering weather forecasts and climate intelligence that people rely on every day to stay safe and grow the economy of the UK. Advancements in space observations are allowing us to improve our weather forecasts and also give us new imagery which helps us show the impacts of other hazards such as wildfires and drought which we have seen this summer.

“Delivering new and innovative space capability is important to enhance our preparedness for extreme weather and exploit the latest advances in our prediction capability using both physics and AI models. We welcome the new UK Space Strategy and its recognition of the vital role space plays in supporting weather and climate services, as well as the Met Office’s role as the UK’s space weather forecasting centre.”

Notes to editors:

The Strategy details how government will go further and faster to develop capability and deliver outcomes in our four priority subsectors:

Satellite Communications

In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing

Space Domain Awareness

Assured Access to Space

The package of space regulatory financial tools contains measures which have been proposed by government, as well as those received in response to the previous consultation on orbital liabilities, insurance, charging and space sustainability . The package covers the following announcements:

Adopting a world-first variable liability limits approach for orbital operations to incentivise uptake of government priorities of security and space sustainability, reduce cost burdens on UK companies and stimulate increased commercial investment in the UK’s space sector.

Waiving operator liability for innovative and novel space missions launched before the end of 2030 (In-Orbit Servicing, Assembly & Manufacturing and lunar missions) to help support development of high potential technologies.

Adoption of new world-first models for the provision of third-party liability insurance to support innovation in the City of London space insurance market.

Abolishing decommissioning funds for operators of constellations in favour of a more proportionate approach to monitoring operators’ financial health.

Further detail on the measures can be found in the government response to the consultation in the link above.

items.title: Sweden to buy HIMARS rocket artillery for around $730 million
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The Swedish government said it needs more rocket artillery fast, signing off on a $733 million purchase of HIMARS weapons from the United States.
items.body:
Europe

Sweden to buy HIMARS rocket artillery for around $730 million

An M142 HIMARS operated by the U.S. Army launches a missile from Palawan, Philippines, during an exercise on Apr. 27, 2026. (Staff Sgt. Brandon Rickert/U.S. Army)

PARIS — Sweden signed off on the purchase of Lockheed Martin’s M142 HIMARS rocket-artillery system for around 7 billion Swedish kronor (US$733 million), with the government saying the security situation is such that it needs rapidly available capabilities to complement its Archer self-propelled howitzers.

The first deliveries of the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System are scheduled for 2027, the Swedish Ministry of Defence said on Monday . Buying the American-produced rocket artillery will allow the Swedish Armed Forces to operate over larger areas and with greater long-range capacity than with the current artillery systems, the ministry said.

“The introduction of rocket artillery clearly demonstrates that Sweden is taking responsibility for security in Europe,” Defense Minister Pål Jonson said.

While Estonia in April expressed concern about possibly delivery delays for HIMARS ammunition due to the Iran war, the Swedish calendar indicates potential bottlenecks may not affect launcher production.

Sweden’s neighboring Norway in January picked Hanwha to supply its Chunmoo rocket artillery system, preferring the South Korean system over HIMARS due to the availability of longer-range munitions.

“The fact that we are now procuring HIMARS and getting long-range precision combat capability on the ground is important not only for the Army but for the Armed Forces as a whole and for our allies,” said Swedish Army chief Maj. Gen. Johan Pekkari in a separate statement .

With Europe currently lacking a home-made equivalent to HIMARS, the Swedish purchase of the U.S. system and Norway acquiring Chunmoo reduces the commercial space for a French rocket artillery system being developed by MBDA and Safran.

The HIMARS systems will be organized in a rocket artillery unit in accordance with plans announced in 2024, Pekkari said. Sweden’s defense bill for the 2025-2030 period , published in 2024, set plans for a rocket artillery unit alongside two Archer battalions.

In parallel with the purchase, Lockheed Martin and Saab are signing a joint declaration on potential integration of Saab’s Ground-Launched Small Diameter Bomb and production of munitions for HIMARS, as well as other systems such as the Patriot air-defense system, the ministry said.

Additionally, Sweden and Finland signed a declaration to cooperate on rocket artillery, including on training, security of supply and production, with Finland’s Multiple Launch Rocket System using the same munitions and components as HIMARS, according to the Swedish ministry.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.
